Let's start by adding Mythras to our research notes and matrices. Here's a basic explanation of the combat to get us started, feel free to do some research on your own to get more information on how the system works when it comes to rules, content, etc. We'll use the other documents as a guide but also use the research to find ideas on how we could expand our system research document template.

Most RPG combat sucks. We've all encountered the same issues. Waiting for your turn is boring. Fights slow to a crawl at high levels. Despite nearly infinite character build options, your choice in combat is limited to whatever hyper-specific level path you're forced to choose. You don't have tactics. You have a button that you push over and over and over every single round. The game simply boils down to which side can deplete the other's resources first. If you've been in one combat, you've been in them all. But what if instead of just chipping away at a bag of hit points, you could break someone's femur into a bag of gravel instead? What if instead of worrying about gaming your AC to absurd height, you always had the fear that someone could slip a knife between your plate armor and cut an artery? What if, as a magic user, having expended all your spells, you could still be in the fight and change the tide of the battle? If you've always wanted your RPG combat to feel like it had real stakes, real choice, and real consequences, then you need to play Mithras. Because this game gives you all of that and so much more. In Mithras, you aren't just stuck waiting for your turn to roll around in the Initiative Order. When you're attacked, you get to do something about it. If you're a magic user, you can still wade into battle swinging a greatsword and cut swaths through your foes. In Mithras gives you all of the system's combat features from the very beginning of the game. Nothing is locked away from behind experienced walls, feet trees, or class restrictions. And while there is serious mechanical depth to the combat system, it's a breeze to use and play. So how does this actually skill system.. work? Mithras is a D100 skill-based system in the tradition of RuneQuest and BRP. When you create your character, you choose a combat style that has a skill rating like any other. Your combat style incorporates all of the different weapons that your character knows how to use, so you don't need to choose individual or group weapon proficiencies to be capable of using most weapons. Like most D100 systems, to use this skill you try to roll under the skill rating in order to succeed. Lower is better and very low is best. So if my combat style rating is 65%, I want to roll 65 or under to succeed. But like I said, if you're being attacked, you don't just have to sit there and take it. Mithras uses opposed rolls, ne success levels.. so while I make an attack against you, you can actively defend against me. Both participants are playing the game at the same time. How this action is resolved is by comparing the results of the rolls and seeing who did better. This is really simple and boils down to seeing the difference in levels of success that each combatant has. When I attacked, did I critically succeed, succeed, fail, or fumble? What about the defender? We compare our results and the difference in success opens up the secret sauce of the Mithras combat system. Special effects. Special effects are fucking awesome. These are maneuvers that are available to everyone from the beginning of the ent to combat.. game and they change the course of combat drastically. For instance, if my attack was a crit and your defense was a failure, I get two levels of success that can be used to apply two special effects against you. So if I attacked you with a spear, I could use the impale special effect to not only get advantage on my damage roll, but to drive the spear through you and leave it stuck in your body. Additionally, I could add the bleed special effect, which means that I severed a blood vessel in addition to any damage. This means if you don't immediately treat the wound, you're going to bleed out and possibly die in a few short rounds. But if the success levels were reversed and my attack was a failure against your critical defense, the defender would get to choose special effects against me. This might include causing me to injure myself with my own weapon and tripping me so that I'm prone until I can't get up on my next turn. Defending yourself from an attack is not a passive act. So even when it's not your turn, you're actually doing something in combat. This makes combat extremely dynamic. And because every character has access to the same pool of maneuvers, players learn the whole combat system very, very quickly. And the game, it just flows. The burden of needing to learn all the permutations of class abilities, feats, and a titanic list of persistent conditions that only gets more burdensome as the levels go up is just gone. Everyone learns one system. The system has a lot of options that can actually be used tactically moment to moment in a fight and keeps you engaged in the excitement of the combat. And while each special effect has its own rules, they're named very clearly without having this specific rule committed to memory. If I wanted to use the overextend opponent special effect, I already sort of have an idea of what it's going to do. I can easily look it up at the table and the game can keep moving without grinding to a halt. Nearly every special effect description is a paragraph of text or less. You don't have to hunt through multiple sections of the book or read a half a page of rules does and how to use it. And on top of that, Mithras uses hit locations, which gives a on.. whole new level of depth to the immersion of the game. If you think hit locations are useless bookkeeping or slow down the game, you are absolutely wrong. This adds so much to role playing. It paints a picture in your mind of exactly what is happening on the battlefield, as well as adding depth to the gameplay itself. If you take a serious wound in your sword arm, you're going to drop your weapon. This is going to make things desperate and heart pumping. Because that's the other thing about Mithras combat. While your skills may increase over time, your hit points don't. While your character may be as fearsome as Conan every time you jump into combat, the adrenaline is going to be pumping because you can be maimed and you can be killed. But death in Mithras doesn't come from depleting a single hit point pool. There are three levels of wounds you can sustain. Minor, serious, and major wounds. Each hit location on your body has its own hit points. Your right arm might have five hit points. A minor wound consists of all the cuts and bruises you'll sustain, which don't pose mortal danger to you. Any damage that doesn't reduce the hit points of a location to zero are all considered a minor wound and do not inflict any additional penalties. If a location goes to zero or lower, you'll take a serious wound and things start getting really bad. If you get hit in the arm, you'll drop your weapon and the limb is now useless. If you get hit in the leg, you'll drop prone. But if you get hit in the head, chest, or abdomen, you may fall unconscious for the rest of the fight. And even if you do survive, you're going to have a horrible scar and long healing process to getting that location functioning properly. But if a location is reduced to a negative score equal to or greater than its starting hit points, that location is instantly severed, pulped, or utterly destroyed. You fall unconscious and possibly even instantly die. That is a major wound. Now, obviously neither you nor anyone else wants to suffer a major wound. This makes combat very deadly and potentially very costly. It means that most fights won't always be to the death and that combat will never drag on for hours and hours at a time. What it does mean is that combat is going to be decisive, take strategy and tactics, and you'll be on the edge of your seat the entire time. And as a GM, this is really, really easy to run, even with less powerful enemies. Not every fight has to be ies that don't require individual tracking of hit locations.. against pure combatants. And if you want your hordes of goobers for your players to wade through without the bookkeeping of tracking hit locations for an entire mob, Mithras has you covered with rabble and underlings. Rabble and underlings are simplified and weaker enemies that don't need individual tracking of all combat parameters. Rabble are generally just mobs of unskilled foes that can't use special effects and either die screaming or run away after sustaining a single wound. Underlings, though, are more dangerous. They can use special effects, just like your players, s before giving up the ghost. Both of these simplified enemies also have morale baked in too, so they're not always just going to slog it out to the death with your player characters, and you don't need to keep track of their hit points by location. But for those fights with iconic enemies, evil monsters, and hated foes, you have a system that's easy to learn, but provides unparalleled depth in the combat experience. And you should build your foes like your player characters to make those battles positively titanic. perative book of foes.. And this is one of the reasons that we chose the orc-licensed Mithras Imperative as the basis of our upcoming supplement, Cults of Zohok. This book has everything that you need to build truly evil and powerful antagonists that your players will demand the opportunity to destroy in battle. You'll find a series of pre-made cults worshipping an ancient evil deity that can be dropped into your fantasy world, and a system of vile black magic that the priests of Zohok used to sew chaos and despair across the land. You'll also get a detailed examination of the idols of Zohok, the terrible golems that these blasphemous cults create and worship, and a full adventure in the city of Avalok where Zohok's influence is corrupting the very soul of the settlement itself. Check the link on screen and in the description to get notified for the upcoming Kickstarter. Mithras has an interesting reputation as being a super crunchy game, and while ot complicated.. that's not untrue, its crunch is not burdensome, and it's not complicated. There's significantly less math to do than in D&D, and the majority of resolving conflicts boils down to comparing the results of opposed die rolls. There is a lot of depth in the combat, but the process is dead simple, and if you can remember this sequence, you'll be able to run it without any issues. 1. Roll initiative to determine turn order. 2. Compare the results of opposed attack and defense rolls. 3. Choose special effects. 4. Determine hit location. 5. Roll damage and apply wounds. This really is simple. If you've been scared off from Mithras because it's described as too crunchy and convoluted, you actually have it completely backwards. Most D&D variants are bloated and complicated. Mithras on the other hand just isn't. You'll learn one very well-made combat system in your early sessions, and then have the ices.. total freedom to roleplay intensely and push the game to the maximum because you don't have to learn more bullshit every single level. And as a game master, you don't need to be responsible for knowing every edge case associated with someone's broken multi-class build or third-party feat tree. Mithras is a unique game. It gives everyone at the table a common set of tools during combat, and doesn't rely on endless subsystems or manipulating the rules to create a perfectly synergized set of named powers siloed in a class. Other games offer you the illusion of choice, by giving enormous decision trees to navigate when you level up, but always end up putting you in a straitjacket based on those choices. Mithras actually gives you meaningful choices that affect the course of a battle in dramatic ways. This gives you a very immersive experience, without sacrificing the gameplay aspects of roleplaying games. Instead of separating these two things, it integrates them. And there's a lot more to the combat system that we didn't cover here. There is a simple action economy, rules for weapon reach, damage reduction through parrying, shields and armor, and a host of actions that can change the course of a fight outside of the use of special effects. It's deep, tactical, and very satisfying. And if d resources for learning more.. you want a taste of Mithras, but aren't ready to jump in quite yet, you can get a simplified version of the core rules in a PDF for free from DriveThruRPG by searching for "Mithras Imperative". But if you are more than a little intrigued and ready to take the Mithras pill, go to the Design Mechanism website and use promo code "BLACKLOG15" for 15% off your order in their bookstore. Mithras is an awesome game that solves all of the bog-standard problems that have plagued RPG combat for decades. Give it a shot and keep your eyes on this channel because we have a lot more to cover on all that Mithras has to offer.

Open Case Study 5: Mythras & The $d100$ Differential Special Effects Engine MD Case Study 5: Mythras & The 𝑑 100 d100 Differential Special Effects Engine To expand our research template and uncover foundational mechanics that can elevate our idealized mathless system, we conducted a deep structural analysis of Mythras (formerly RuneQuest 6, developed by Lawrence Whitaker and Pete Nash at The Design Mechanism). Mythras represents the pinnacle of grounded, simulationist d100 combat design. It proves that tactical depth and dramatic stakes do not require class-locked feat trees, escalating 𝐻 𝑃 HP bloat, or mathematical modifier inflation. 1. Core Architectural Pillars of Mythras 1.1 The 𝑑 100 d100 Opposed Check & Differential Levels of Success Unlike passive combat engines where an attacker rolls against a static Armor Class ( 𝐴 𝐶 AC), combat in Mythras is actively opposed. Both attacker and defender roll simultaneously ( 𝑑 100 d100 percentile roll under their respective Combat Style % or Evade %). Every roll achieves one of four Levels of Success: Critical Success: Rolling ≤ 1 / 10 th ≤1/10th of the skill rating (e.g., Skill 65 % → 65%→ Crit on 1 - 7 1-7). Standard Success: Rolling between critical threshold and the skill rating ( ≤ 65 % ≤65%). Standard Failure: Rolling above skill rating ( 66 - 98 % 66-98%). Fumble: Rolling 99 - 00 99-00. Instead of merely checking who hit or missed, Mythras compares the difference in success levels between the combatants. If my attack is a Critical Success (Level 4) and your parry is a Standard Failure (Level 2), I win by Two Levels of Success ( 4 − 2 = 2 4−2=2). text [ Attacker: Critical Success (Level 4) ] vs [ Defender: Standard Failure (Level 2) ] │ ▼ [ Differential: +2 Levels of Success ] │ ┌────────────────────┴────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ [ Spend Level 1: Impale ] [ Spend Level 2: Bleed ] (Drive spear deep; weapon stuck) (Sever artery; rapid blood loss) 1.2 Universal Special Effects (Maneuvers Without Class Walls) The "secret sauce" of Mythras is what you do with those differential levels of success: Special Effects. Whenever a combatant wins an opposed roll by 1 or 2 levels of success, they immediately spend those differential levels to choose from a universal catalog of Special Effects. No Class Restrictions or Level Gates: A starting character on turn one has access to the exact same pool of maneuvers as a seasoned veteran. If you achieve a critical hit over a failed parry, you don't need a level 12 "Impaling Feat"; you simply choose Impale right at the table. Active Defense Turns the Tables: If the attacker misses (Failure) and the defender succeeds (Critical Success or Success), the defender gains Special Effects against the attacker. A parrying warrior can instantly Disarm, Overextend, Trip, or Riposte their attacker out-of-turn. 2. Mythras Special Effects Catalog (Offensive vs Defensive) Every maneuver is succinctly defined in a paragraph or less, allowing rapid table execution: 2.1 Sample Offensive Special Effects Impale: Drives a piercing weapon deep into the target. Deals maximum weapon damage or rolls twice, and the weapon remains wedged inside, inflicting agonizing pain (penalties to all actions) until wrenched free (causing secondary damage). Bleed: Severs a major blood vessel. The target loses 1 1 or 2 2 Fatigue/HP at the start of every turn until medically sutured or coagulated. Bypass Armor: The strike slips through a gap in plate armor or thick hide (e.g., eye slit, armpit). The target's armor Damage Reduction ( 𝐷 𝑅 DR) is completely ignored for this hit. Compel Surrender: Instead of striking a lethal blow, the victor holds their blade to the opponent's throat or eye, forcing an immediate morale/surrender check before blood is shed. Maximize Damage: The kinetic blow strikes squarely on bone. All weapon damage dice automatically yield their maximum face value. Stun / Bash: A heavy blunt strike rattles the brain or nervous system. Target must pass a Endurance check or drop incapacitated for 1 𝑑 4 1d4 rounds. 2.2 Sample Defensive Special Effects (Earned via Successful Parry/Evade over Attack) Overextend Opponent: The defender redirects the attacker’s momentum off-balance. The attacker suffers an immediate penalty on their next defensive roll or loses an Action Point ( 𝐴 𝑃 AP). Disarm: The defender catches the attacker’s blade with a crossguard or shield rim, wrenching it out of their hands (opposed Brawn/Strength check to retain). Trip / Drop Foe: A quick foot-sweep or shield bash sends the attacker sprawling Prone. Riposte: If the parry was a Critical Success against a Failure, the defender gets a free, immediate counter-attack strike that cannot be parried. Damage Weapon: The defender angles their heavy shield or hardened blade to catch the opponent's weapon shaft, inflicting direct structural damage (Hardness/Hit Points) to break the incoming weapon. 3. Hit Locations & The 3-Tier Anatomical Wound System While most games track a single abstract bar of 100 + 100+ Hit Points, Mythras uses Localized Hit Locations (Head 13-20, Chest 09-12, Abdomen 07-08, Left Arm 04-06, Right Arm 01-03, Left Leg/Right Leg). 3.1 Static HP & Armor Soak per Location Each location has its own static pool of Hit Points based on character Size and Constitution (e.g., Head = 5 HP, Chest = 7 HP, Arm = 4 HP). These points do NOT scale with character advancement. A veteran warrior has roughly the same anatomical HP as a novice. Armor applies local Damage Reduction ( 𝐷 𝑅 DR) only to the location it covers (e.g., Steel breastplate = +6 DR on Chest; Leather bracers = +2 DR on Arms). 3.2 The Three Wound Levels When damage overcomes armor 𝐷 𝑅 DR, it depletes the local Hit Points and triggers one of three concrete wound states: Wound Level Local HP Formula Anatomical Consequence & Narrative Reality 1. Minor Wound Local HP > 0 Standard cuts, bruises, and kinetic shock. Causes pain and minor bleeding, but no structural impairment. 2. Serious Wound Local HP <= 0
(but > -Starting HP) Structural failure of the limb or organ. If an Arm, the limb goes limp (Drop weapon/shield). If a Leg, target falls Prone (Cannot stand/run). If Head, Chest, or Abdomen, target collapses Unconscious and must make Endurance rolls to avoid bleeding out. 3. Major Wound Local HP <= -Starting HP
(Negative local max) Catastrophic Severance & Destruction. An Arm or Leg is cleanly severed or crushed beyond repair (Instant shock, permanent loss). If Head, Chest, or Abdomen, the skull is crushed or heart punctured → → Instant Death. 4. Action Points (AP) & Defensive Action Economy In Mythras, survival is governed by the Action Point ( 𝐴 𝑃 AP) Budget: Characters typically possess 2 or 3 Action Points ( 𝐴 𝑃 AP) per combat round. Active Defense Costs 𝐴 𝑃 AP: Every offensive strike costs 1 𝐴 𝑃 1AP. Crucially, every active Parry or Evade also costs 1 𝐴 𝑃 1AP. The Outnumbering Dilemma: If you are attacked by three foes and spend all your 𝐴 𝑃 AP parrying the first two strikes, you have zero 𝐴 𝑃 AP left when the third strike arrives. You cannot actively parry or evade; you must rely entirely on passive armor 𝐷 𝑅 DR and luck (Automatic hit against your location). This makes tactical positioning, shield walls, and outnumbering enemies matter deeply without artificial math. 5. Each extra beating die awards 1 Mathless Special Effect Token ([SET]) (2 beating dice = 1 standard hit + 1 Special Effect). Trigger 2 (Max Face Surge): Rolling the maximum face value (8 on 𝑑 8 d8) automatically awards +1 Special Effect Token ([SET]). These tokens ([SET]) are spent instantly from our universal table (Impale, Bleed, Disarm, Overextend, Riposte) without checking class prerequisites! If targeted by additional attacks beyond that slot, they must burn 1 Stamina per active parry/evade (Parry Fatigue). If they run out of Stamina, they cannot parry, leaving their physical Soak Rank as their only line of defense. When an attack beats Soak by ≥ 1 ≥1 step (Severe Wound), the player or GM rolls a single Anatomical Location Die ( 1 𝑑 8 1d8) (1-2 Head, 3-4 Chest, 5 Abdomen, 6-7 Arms, 8 Legs) to apply localized structural impairments (Dropped weapon, Prone, Concussion) without adding numerical HP bookkeeping. Rabble & Underling Mob Management: We adopt exact Mythras mob tiers for GMs: Rabble die on any hit exceeding Soak; Underlings use Special Effects but collapse after 1 severe wound; Iconic Bosses use full multi-layer defenses and anatomical wound clocks. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Simulate Boons with mixed step dice to test granularity vs redundancy.
"""
import itertools

dice = [4, 6, 8, 10, 12]
dcs = [3, 5, 7, 9, 11]

def get_step_down(d):
    idx = dice.index(d)
    return dice[max(0, idx - 1)]

def get_step_up(d):
    idx = dice.index(d)
    return dice[min(len(dice) - 1, idx + 1)]

def prob_pool(pool, dc):
    if max(pool) < dc:
        return 0.0
    total = 1
    for d in pool:
        total *= d
    successes = sum(1 for roll in itertools.product(*[range(1, d + 1) for d in pool]) if max(roll) >= dc)
    return (successes / total) * 100.0

def main():
    print("=== PROBABILITY OF HITTING TARGET DC (%) ===")
    for base in dice:
        print(f"\n--- Base Die: d{base} ---")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Simulate Competency Floors (Fixed Die Floor) across the 5 Competency Levels over 20 levels.
Evaluates both Fixed DC Success Rates (%) and Opposed Roll Win/Tie/Loss Rates (%).
"""
import itertools

# Define the 5 Competency Levels across the 20 levels
# Format: (Name, Die Size, Pool Volume, Competency Floor)
COMPETENCY_LEVELS = [
    ("0. Untrained (Lvl 0 Civilian)", 6, 2, 0),
    ("1. Trained (Tier 1 Lvl 1-4)", 8, 3, 3),
    ("2. Expert (Tier 2 Lvl 5-8)", 10, 3, 5),
    ("3. Master (Tier 3/4 Lvl 9-15)", 12, 4, 7),
    ("4. Legendary (Tier 5/6 Lvl 16+)", 12, 5, 9)
]

DCS = [3, 5, 7, 9, 11]

def simulate_fixed_dcs():
    print("=== PART 1: FIXED DC SUCCESS RATES WITH COMPETENCY FLOORS (%) ===")
    header = f"{'Competency Level':<35}" + "".join([f"DC {dc}:<8" for dc in DCS])
    print(header)
    print("-" * len(header))
    
    for name, die, num_dice, floor in COMPETENCY_LEVELS:
        row = f"{name:<35}"
        total_outcomes = die ** num_dice
        for dc in DCS:
            if floor >= dc:
                row += f"{'100.0%':<8}"
            elif die < dc:
                row += f"{'0.0%':<8}"
            else:
                successes = sum(
                    1 for roll in itertools.product(range(1, die + 1), repeat=num_dice)
                    if max(max(roll), floor) >= dc
                )
                prob = (successes / total_outcomes) * 100.0
                row += f"{prob:<7.1f}% "
        print(row)

def simulate_opposed_contests():

    print(header)

    # Select key matchups to demonstrate differential floors

        (2, 1), # Expert vs Trained
        (3, 2), # Master vs Expert
        (4, 3), # Legendary vs Master
        (4, 0), # Legendary vs Untrained (Total Dominance)
        (1, 1), # Trained vs Trained (Mirror Match)
        (2, 2), # Expert vs Expert (Mirror Match)
        (3, 3), # Master vs Master (Mirror Match)
        (1, 2), # Trained vs Expert (Underdog)
    ]
    
    for att_idx, def_idx in matchups:

        def_name, def_die, def_num, def_floor = COMPETENCY_LEVELS[def_idx]

        # Since 12^5 * 12^4 = 248,832 * 20,736 = ~5 billion outcomes, Monte Carlo 150,000 trials is extremely accurate!
        import random

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Simulate Paired Defense Pools (e.g., DEX + INT for Reflexes, STR + CON for Fortitude, WIS + CHA for Willpower)
across 5 Investment Configurations vs Fixed DCs and Equivalent Offense Pools.
"""
import itertools
import random

# Define the 5 Defense Investment Configurations
# Format: (Config Name, Attr1 Die, Attr2 Die, Extra Boons on Highest Attr, Competency Floor)
DEFENSE_CONFIGS = [
    ("1. Zero Investment on Either (d6 + d6)", 6, 6, 0, 0),
    ("2. Avg Investment on ONE (d10 + d6, +1B)", 10, 6, 1, 3),
    ("3. Avg Investment on BOTH (d8 + d8, +1B)", 8, 8, 1, 3),
    ("4. Max Investment on ONE (d12 + d6, +2B)", 12, 6, 2, 7),
    ("5. Max Investment on BOTH (d12 + d12, +2B)", 12, 12, 2, 7)
]

DCS = [3, 5, 7, 9, 11]

def build_pool(attr1, attr2, boons):
    """Builds the paired defense dice pool."""
    pool = [attr1, attr2]
    highest = max(attr1, attr2)
    for _ in range(boons):
        pool.append(highest)
    return pool

def simulate_fixed_dcs():
    print("=== PART 1: PAIRED DEFENSE POOL SUCCESS RATES vs FIXED DCs (%) ===")
    header = f"{'Defense Configuration':<44}" + "".join([f"DC {dc}:<8" for dc in DCS])
    print(header)
    print("-" * len(header))
    
    for name, a1, a2, boons, floor in DEFENSE_CONFIGS:
        pool = build_pool(a1, a2, boons)
        row = f"{name:<44}"
        total_outcomes = 1
        for d in pool:
            total_outcomes *= d
            
        for dc in DCS:
            if floor >= dc:
                row += f"{'100.0%':<8}"
            elif max(pool) < dc:
                row += f"{'0.0%':<8}"
            else:
                successes = sum(
                    1 for roll in itertools.product(*[range(1, d + 1) for d in pool])
                    if max(max(roll), floor) >= dc
                )
                prob = (successes / total_outcomes) * 100.0
                row += f"{prob:<7.1f}% "
        print(row)

def simulate_opposed_contests():
    print("\n=== PART 2: OPPOSED CONTESTS vs EQUIVALENT OFFENSE POOLS ===")
    print("Compares Paired Defense Pool vs Attacker Pool (Att Win % | Def Win/Save % | Exact Tie %)")
    print("-" * 88)
    
    # Define Equivalent Offense Tiers to test against
    # Format: (Offense Label, Attacker Pool Dice, Attacker Floor)
    offense_tiers = [
        ("Tier 1 Offense (3d8, Floor 3)", [8, 8, 8], 3),
        ("Tier 2 Offense (3d10, Floor 5)", [10, 10, 10], 5),
        ("Tier 3/4 Offense (4d12, Floor 7)", [12, 12, 12, 12], 7)
    ]
    
    random.seed(42)
    trials = 100000
    
    for off_label, att_pool, att_floor in offense_tiers:
        print(f"\n>>> Against {off_label}:")
        header = f"{'Defender Configuration':<44} | Att Win % | Def Save % | Exact Tie %"
        print(header)
        print("-" * len(header))
        
        for name, a1, a2, boons, def_floor in DEFENSE_CONFIGS:
            def_pool = build_pool(a1, a2, boons)
            
            att_wins = 0
            def_wins = 0
            ties = 0
            
            for _ in range(trials):
                # Roll Attacker
                att_roll = max(random.randint(1, d) for d in att_pool)
                att_roll = max(att_roll, att_floor)
                
                # Roll Defender
                def_roll = max(random.randint(1, d) for d in def_pool)
                def_roll = max(def_roll, def_floor)
                
                if att_roll > def_roll:
                    att_wins += 1
                elif def_roll > att_roll:
                    def_wins += 1
                else:
                    ties += 1
                    
            short_name = name.split(" (")[0] + f" ({a1}+{a2})"
            print(f"{short_name:<44} | {att_wins/trials*100:<9.1f}% | {def_wins/trials*100:<10.1f}% | {ties/trials*100:<7.1f}%")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    simulate_fixed_dcs()
    simulate_opposed_contests()

🏛️ The Two Cleanest Ways to Map "Everything Else"

To finalize how a player builds and rolls their pool from their Race + Class + Skills (Competency Ranks) + Feats, we have two primary architectural options:

Option 1: The "Pure Role Separation" Model (Cleanest & Most Intuitive)

→

0. Untrained (Civilian): Roll 2dX keep highest, Floor = 0 (Pure random 2-die roll).
1. Trained (Basic Hero): Roll 3dX keep highest (+1 die boon), Floor = 3.
2. Expert (Specialist): Roll 3dX keep highest (+1 die boon), Floor = 5 (Guaranteed immunity to standard DC 5 misses).
3. Master (Grandmaster): Roll 4dX keep highest (+2 dice boons), Floor = 7.
4. Legendary (Paragon): Roll 5dX keep highest (+3 dice boons — Maximum Pool Cap), Floor = 9.

→

Your Class dictates how easily you buy Competency Ranks (e.g., Fighters start Trained in Combat at Level 1), and gives you active feats (Power Strike [1A], Cleave [0A], Riposte [SET]).

In this model (which we explored in our earlier progression checks), we split things across both axes:

Die Size (X): Governed by Core Attribute (STR d8) + Competency Rank Step Upgrades (Untrained = +0 steps, Trained = +1 Die Step-Up to d10, Master = +2 Die Step-Ups to d12).
Pool Volume (Dice Count): Governed by your Class Baseline (Martial Class = Base 3 dice, Civilian/Caster Class = Base 2 dice) plus Tactical Situations (Flanking +1 die, High Ground +1 die).
Competency Floor (F): Governed by your Competency Rank (0, 3, 5, 7, 9).

Schwalb’s Shadow of the Demon Lord (SotDL) and Shadow of the Weird Wizard serve as our secondary architectural anchors. While SotDL revolutionized modern d20 design by replacing static numerical modifiers (+2 / -2) with dynamic Boons and Banes (Nd6) and introducing modular 3-Tier Paths, our system inherits its structural elegance and evolves it beyond table-side arithmetic into a full Mathless Step-Pool Engine. This document compares our 8-Block Progression Ecosystem against SotDL across six architectural dimensions and provides exact side-by-side conversion and combat comparisons. 1. Architectural Comparison Matrix (SotDL vs. Our Mathless System) Architectural Dimension Shadow of the Demon Lord (SotDL / Weird Wizard) Our Idealized Mathless System (Evolution & Upgrade) Why Our System Elevates Simulationism & Flow 1. Resolution Formula & Table Arithmetic 1 𝑑 20 + Attribute Mod ± Highest of  𝑁 𝑑 6 1d20+Attribute Mod±Highest of Nd6 (Boons/Banes).
Requires table arithmetic on every check (e.g., d20 roll [14] + Str mod [+3] + highest boon d6 [+5] = 22 vs Defense 16). NdX keep highest (Step Pools with Zero Math).
Attribute + Competency sets Die Size (X); Class + Boons sets Pool Volume (N). You roll the pool and compare highest face directly against Target DC or opposed die (max vs max). Zero Arithmetic Latency. Eliminates linear addition equations completely ($d20 \pm d6$), delivering immediate visual clarity the moment dice stop spinning (DEC-001). 2. Boons & Banes Mechanism Additive Extra Dice (Nd6). Boons add 𝑁 𝑑 6 Nd6 (keep highest d6 and ADD to d20). Banes add 𝑁 𝑑 6 Nd6 (keep highest d6 and SUBTRACT from d20). They cancel 1-to-1 before rolling. Pool Volume Shifts (+1B / +1X). Boons add extra dice of the same step size directly to your check pool (+1B -> 3dX keep highest). Banes remove dice (+1X -> 1dX single roll). They cancel 1-to-1 (DEC-003). Preserves SotDL’s brilliant 1-to-1 cancellation without reintroducing table-side arithmetic or mixing multi-size dice (DEC-017). 3. Progression & Class Structure 3-Tier Path Layering (10 Levels Total).
• Novice Path (Lvl 1-2): Core role (Warrior, Priest).
• Expert Path (Lvl 3-6): Profession (Berserker, Paladin).
• Master Path (Lvl 7-10): High concept (Blade Dancer). 6-Tier Path Layering across 20 Levels (and Epic 21+).
We expand SotDL's paths into 4-level bands across 6 High Fantasy Tiers (Trained Lvl 1-4 -> Veteran Lvl 5-8 -> Master Lvl 9-12 -> Hero Lvl 13-16 -> Legend Lvl 17-20 -> Mythic Lvl 21+). Applied universally to PCs and Monsters (DEC-011). Combines SotDL’s modular path selection (zero dead levels or prerequisite traps) with D&D 3.5e/PF2e’s granular level-by-level growth across 20 levels (DEC-013). 4. Skill & Competency Granularity Freeform Professions (No Skill Lists). Players list professions (e.g., Blacksmith, Sailor). If relevant to a check, GM awards + 1  Boon (‘+1d6‘) +1 Boon (‘+1d6‘) (or +2 Boons). 5 Action Mastery Domains (Combat, Survival, Subterfuge, Lore, Social) & 5 Competency Ranks (Untrained 0 to Legendary 9).
Advancing competency steps up Die Size (X+1 to X+3), increases Pool Volume (+1B to +3B), and sets Competency Floors (Fixed Die Minimums). SotDL professions lack advancement (a Blacksmith at Lvl 1 gets +1 Boon; at Lvl 10 still gets +1 Boon). Our Competency Ranks give explicit, investment-driven growth where experts literally cannot whiff on routine checks (DEC-019). 5. Defense & Mitigation Model Single Passive Defense Score (10 to 18). If light/unarmored, Defense = Agility. Heavy armor (Plate = Defense 17) completely overrides and replaces Agility. Damage drains a single linear Health bar. 4 Paired Defensive Layers (Reflexes DEX+INT, Parry Combat Pool, Resilience Fort/Will, and Soak Rank Armor Die).

This overview serves as our design baseline to review, trim, or refactor specific subsystems (such as streamlining Special Effect Tokens [SET] or adjusting how HP/Vitality works). 1. Core Philosophy & Universal Actor Schema High Fantasy Baseline (DEC-014): Level 1 characters start as Trained Heroes (above average civilian baselines). They are competent professionals capable of reliable execution and heroic survival. Strictly Zero Table-Side Arithmetic (DEC-001): Action resolution compares rolled die face values (d4 to d12+) directly against Target Numbers (DCs 2 to 12) or opposed die faces (max vs max). There is zero addition or subtraction of linear numerical modifiers (no +BAB, no +Stat mod, no -4 Power Attack). Strictly Zero Meta-Currencies (DEC-006): All heroic luck, effort, and survival run strictly on in-world character tracks (Stamina, Focus, and Equipment Durability Sacrifices). Universal Actor Schema (DEC-011): Every single entity in the game world (PCs, human NPCs, Goblins, Ogres, Dragons) is built from the exact same four foundational blocks: Actor Block = Race / Ancestry + Class Levels (‘1-20 across 6 Tiers‘) + Skills (‘Competency Ranks‘) + Feats (‘Vector Traits‘) Actor Block=Race / Ancestry+Class Levels (‘1-20 across 6 Tiers‘)+Skills (‘Competency Ranks‘)+Feats (‘Vector Traits‘) 2. Alright. We'll do some more fundamental changes.

Competency Ranks: The definition that it "measure specific player investment in one of the 5 Action Mastery Domains" is correct, but each domain should not be a single thing the player can invest in, since that would be way too abstracted. Walking silently and hiding from view should be two different things, as should be knowing about dragons vs knowing about bears, as well as convincing through intimidation vs lying vs being diplomatic, etc.

Action Economy & Turn Structure: Let's call the distance tiers 0 Close, 1 Near, 2 Medium, 4 Far, 4 Distant.

In-World Resources & Daily Pacing: I like Stamina and Focus, but we will still have a "Vancian" casting system, so casting a spell doesn't necessarily need focus by default, only for other secondary reasons.

Durability Slots: How would this compare to D&D 3.5e's item HP, hardness, and Sundering?

Encumbrance Slots: We should base this on both STR and CON, much like vitality.

Hit Location & Anatomical Wound Severance: Wouldn't a crit being Damage rolled Max Face mean that higher dice have a lower change of critting? Maybe we could use D&D 3.5e as inspiration. Weapons have a crit profile (% chance for crit) and the player rolls a d100 with their dice pool to see if they crit.

Wounds should only happen on a Crit, although normal hits could have minor disrupting effects that can be quickly resolved with the right Class Abilities, Feats, etc.

A player should be able to force a wound (and its effect) by using a Called Shot maneuver at some cost.

Edited files 2 Master Executive Summary: Top-to-Bottom System Architecture MD Master Executive Summary: Top-to-Bottom System Architecture This document provides a concise, comprehensive, top-to-bottom briefing of our Idealized Mathless High Fantasy TTRPG System (as of Decision DEC-035). It consolidates all mechanics, progression tracks, check engines, combat layers, and resource pools into a single unified view. This overview serves as our definitive design baseline to review, trim, or refactor specific subsystems (such as streamlining quick disruptions or adjusting specific class talents). 1. Core Philosophy & Universal Actor Schema High Fantasy Baseline (DEC-014): Level 1 characters start as Trained Heroes (above average civilian baselines). They are competent professionals capable of reliable execution and heroic survival. Strictly Zero Table-Side Arithmetic (DEC-001): Action resolution compares rolled die face values (d4 to d12+) directly against Target Numbers (DCs 2 to 12) or opposed die faces (max vs max). There is zero addition or subtraction of linear numerical modifiers (no +BAB, no +Stat mod, no -4 Power Attack). Strictly Zero Meta-Currencies (DEC-006): All heroic luck, effort, and survival run strictly on in-world character tracks (Stamina, Focus, Vancian Spell Slots, and Equipment Durability Sacrifices). Universal Actor Schema (DEC-011): Every single entity in the game world (PCs, human NPCs, Goblins, Ogres, Dragons) is built from the exact same four foundational blocks: Actor Block = Race / Ancestry + Class Levels (‘1-20 across 6 Tiers‘) + Skills (‘Specific Allocations‘) + Feats (‘Vector Traits‘) Actor Block=Race / Ancestry+Class Levels (‘1-20 across 6 Tiers‘)+Skills (‘Specific Allocations‘)+Feats (‘Vector Traits‘) 2. The Check Engine (Tri-Vector Pools & Competency Floors) When any actor declares a check or attack, their dice pool (NdX keep highest) is generated by three variables: text [ Assembling a Check Pool: The 3 Mechanical Variables ] ├── 1. Die Size (`X` — d4 to d12+) ──────────────► Governs Capability Ceiling & Impact (`Core Attribute + Competency Step Shift`) ├── 2. Pool Volume (`N` — 1d to 5d) ─────────────► Governs Reliability & Multi-Beat Count (`Base 2d + Class Boon + Tactical Boons`) └── 3. Competency Floor (`F` — 0, 3, 5, 7, 9) ──► Governs Guaranteed Minimum Face (`Investment-Driven Whiff Immunity`) 2.1 Competency Ranks (Specific Skills under 5 Umbrellas — DEC-020 & DEC-030) Competency Ranks measure specific player investment in Individual Specific Skills (Stealth, Lockpicking, Arcana, Nature, Diplomacy, Blades, Bows) grouped under our 5 Action Mastery Domain Umbrellas (Combat, Survival, Subterfuge, Lore, Social), independent of overall character level: 0. Untrained (Zero Investment): Base Pool 2dX keep highest, Floor = 0 (Can whiff on routine tasks). 1. Trained (Basic Professional Focus): Pool Volume 3dX (+1B), Floor = 3 (100% immune to failing DC 3). 2. Expert (Dedicated Specialization): Pool Volume 3dX (+1B) + 1 Die Step-Up (X+1), Floor = 5 (100% immune to failing DC 5). 3. Master (Elite Grandmastery): Pool Volume 4dX (+2B) + 2 Die Step-Ups (X+2), Floor = 7 (100% immune to failing DC 7). 4. Legendary (Mythic Apex): Pool Volume 5dX (+3B — Max Pool Cap) + 3 Die Step-Ups (X+3), Floor = 9 (100% immune to failing DC 9). 2.2 Boons, Banes & Die Stepping (DEC-016 & DEC-017) Boons (+1B, +2B) & Banes (+1X, +2X): Adjust Pool Volume only (N) by adding or removing dice of the SAME SIZE (2d8 + 1B -> 3d8 keep highest). Banes remove dice (2d8 + 1X -> 1d8 single roll; +2X -> 2d8 keep lowest / Disadvantage). They cancel 1-to-1 before rolling. Max pool ceiling is 5dX. Die Step-Up (X+1) & Step-Down (X-1): Adjust Die Size only (X). Spending 1 Stamina (or Focus) performs an on-demand Die Step-Up (e.g., 2d6 -> 2d8) to overcome hard DC ceilings or push physical limits. Over-encumbrance or exhaustion imposes a Die Step-Down (d10 -> d8). 3. The Three Check Modes (Tri-Modal Resolution — DEC-015) The Game Master applies the appropriate resolution engine based on intuitive battlefield reality: Check Mode Core Comparison Formula When to Apply (Intuitive Trigger) Action Examples Mode 1: Fixed DC max ⁡ ( Pool ) ≥ Static DC (‘2 to 12‘) max(Pool)≥Static DC (‘2 to 12‘) Static obstacles, environmental hazards, downtime crafting clocks, and uncontested feats. Climbing a sheer cliff (DC 7), picking an unattended master lock (DC 8), forging a steel blade (DC 5). Mode 2: Pure Opposed max ⁡ ( Attacker ) > max ⁡ ( Defender ) max(Attacker)>max(Defender) Dynamic, chaotic clashing between two active opponents where difficulty is purely opponent effort. Melee combat strikes where defender actively parries/evades (Combat vs Parry), wrestling/grappling, active stealth vs searching. Mode 3: Hybrid (DC Floor) max ⁡ ( Attacker ) > max ⁡ ( Defender ) max(Attacker)>max(Defender)
AND max ⁡ ( Attacker ) ≥ DC Floor max(Attacker)≥DC Floor Complex, technical actions carrying an intrinsic physical/spatial difficulty floor against active resistance. Ranged attacks at extreme distance / heavy cover (Must beat Evasion AND clear Distance DC Floor), channeling high-tier spells against target Resilience (Must beat Resilience AND clear Spell Complexity Floor). 4. Attributes & Paired Defenses (DEC-021 & DEC-022) Characters possess the Classic Six Ability Scores (STR, DEX, CON, INT, WIS, CHA) as step dice (d4 to d12+). Two paired attributes combine directly to form the baseline check pool (1dAttr1 + 1dAttr2 keep highest) for our three saving throw defense layers: text [ Classic 6 Ability Scores ] ──────────► [ Derived Paired Defense Pool (`1dAttr1 + 1dAttr2 keep highest`) ] ├── Strength (STR) + Constitution (CON) ──► Fortitude Pool (`Purely Physical Resilience vs Poisons/Disease`) ├── Dexterity (DEX) + Intelligence (INT) ──► Reflexes Pool (`Hybrid Physical + Mental Evasion vs Fireballs/AoE`) └── Wisdom (WIS) + Charisma (CHA) ──► Willpower Pool (`Purely Mental/Spiritual Resilience vs Mind Blasts/Curses`) Good vs. Poor Class Saves (DEC-029 Track 3): If a class has a Good Save in 3.5e (e.g., Fighter Fortitude, Wizard Willpower), the class awards +1B (+1 die volume -> 3dX) at Level 1, and elevates to +2B (4dX, Floor 5/7) at Level 9 (Master Tier Entry). Poor saves roll standard 2dX paired pools (Floor 0/3). 5. Action Economy & Turn Structure (DEC-008 & DEC-031) 3-Action Turn Budget ([A][A][A]): On their turn, characters spend 3 action points flexibly across Single Actions ([1A] Stride, Strike, Raise Guard), Two-Action Activities ([2A] Cast Spell, Sudden Charge), or Three-Action Surges ([3A] Whirlwind Strike). Multi-Attack Fatigue: Making multiple physical attacks on the same turn imposes Stamina/Pool Fatigue (+1 Bane Die on 2nd attack, +2 Banes on 3rd), eliminating 3.5e's − 5 / − 10 −5/−10 subtraction and stationary full-attack paralysis. Active Defense Budget ([1R] + Stamina Burn): Every character gets 1 Free Defensive Reaction ([1R]) per round (Active Parry or Shield Intercept). Additional active parries/evades against swarming enemies cost 1 Stamina per attempt (Parry Fatigue). When Stamina hits 0 0, active defense collapses (Parry Pool = 0), forcing reliance on passive armor Soak! In-World Resources & Daily Pacing (DEC-006, DEC-032, DEC-033) Six concrete in-world tracks govern character lifespan, exertion, and camp tension across a Dual-Frequency Pacing Model: Resource Track Derivation & Maximum Capacity Depletion Triggers Recovery Rule (10-Minute Breather vs. 8-Hour Camp) 1. Vitality (HP) STR Die Max + CON Die Max
(e.g., 8 + 10 = 18  Base Vitality 8+10=18 Base Vitality).
Advances via bounded class increments (+2 HP Good, +1 Okay) at odd levels (3, 5, 7...). Weapon strikes exceeding Soak Rank (Damage > Soak), environmental hazards, falling, blood loss. Advances via bounded class increments (+2 Stamina Martial, +1 Caster) at even levels (2, 6, 10...). 🏛️ The Swapped Model (Model B) vs. Our Locked Baseline (Model A)
Why Swapping (Model B) Was a Fascinating Consideration

If we had swapped so that Attribute = Pool Volume (N — e.g., STR 4 = 4 dice) and Level = Die Size (X — Lvl 1=d6, Lvl 5=d8, Lvl 9=d10, Lvl 15=d12):

The Major Pro: It gives 100% rigid, foolproof DC bounding by level. At Level 1, literally no character can naturally clear DC 7 (because all Level 1 characters roll d6s). At Level 5, the entire party's ceiling steps up to d8. And grabbing dice (STR 3 + Blades 2 = 5 dice -> 5d) uses ultra-fast table math.
The Major Simulationist Con: Because your level strictly dictates your die size, a Level 1 Ogre Brute (STR 5) and a Level 1 Halfling Rogue (STR 2) both roll d6s when striking someone. The Ogre hits vastly more often (5d6 vs 2d6), but his raw kinetic ceiling (max damage face 6) is identical to the Halfling's until we apply a heavy racial step override.
Why Locking In Model A (DEC-038) + Background Focus (DEC-039) is Superior

By keeping Model A (Core Attribute = Die Size X | Competency Rank = Pool Volume N and Floor F) while automating core role growth through the Background Focus, we get exact physical realism without any risk of a "trap build":

What is this [SET] token deal?

[SET] stands for "Special Effect Tokens" (or "Maneuver Tokens").

It was our initial mechanism for adapting Mythras’s differential combat maneuvers (Case Study 5) into our mathless step-pool engine.

🔍 Exactly What [SET] Is Right Now (And How It Works)

In Mythras, whenever an attacker beats a defender's parry by 1 or 2 levels of success (e.g., Critical vs. Failure), the winner immediately earns 1 or 2 "Special Effects" that they can spend right at the table to perform maneuvers (Impale, Bleed, Disarm, Trip, Riposte) without needing class feats.

Multi-Success Maneuvers & Pool Trade-offs (No Tokens — DEC-042 & DEC-043) To eliminate token counting currencies ([SET]) while preserving dynamic, universal combat maneuvers (Mythras tradition), maneuvers are executed directly using Multi-Success Counts (Required Successes S) and Check Pool Trade-offs (+1 Bane Die). 7.1 Multi-Success Combat Triggers (Zero Tokens) When making an opposed attack check (Attacker Pool vs Defender Parry/Reflexes Pool), compare how many of your rolled dice equal or exceed the defender's highest face (Multi-Beat Count): 1 Success (Highest face beats defender): Standard Hit (Damage vs Absorption). Can inflict quick minor disruptions (Bleeding Cut, Shaken). Does not force Prone, Disarm, or Anatomical Wounds. 2 Successes (Two dice independently equal/exceed defender's highest face): Superior Hit (Standard Hit + 1 Universal Maneuver). You automatically execute 1 universal maneuver (Trip, Disarm, Shove, Overextend) right off the dice! 3+ Successes (Three dice equal/exceed defender's highest face): Overwhelming Hit (Standard Hit + Major Maneuver OR 2 Maneuvers). Attacker deals normal Damage vs Absorption AND immediately trips the target Prone AND disarms their weapon instantly without counting tokens! 7.2 Universal Default Maneuvers (Belong to Everyone) Universal default maneuvers are not hardcoded to specific weapons; they exist for all actors (PCs, NPCs, Monsters). If your check pool yields 2+ Successes, the maneuver happens for free! Knob B (Pool Volume Trade-off / +1 Bane Die): Declare the maneuver before rolling (say, [1A] Disarm Strike). You accept $+1\text{ Bane Die (-1 die volume: 4d10 → → 3d10)}$ on your check. If your highest face wins (just 1 Success required), the maneuver happens automatically! Knob C (Dedicated Action Check): Spend a dedicated action point ([1A] Maneuver check like an opposed Athletics shove/disarm without damage) OR make a 2-action sure-strike activity ([2A] Precision Maneuver). 8. The Three Check Modes (Fixed DC vs Pure Opposed vs Hybrid DC Floor) To ensure resolution is always ground-in reality and intuitive for the Game Master, our system natively supports All Three Modes of Resolution. The GM applies each where it makes sense from an intuition standpoint: text [ What is the nature of the challenge? ] │ ┌─────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ [ Static Obstacle / Crafting ] [ Active Melee / Social ] [ Long Range / Technical Spell ] │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Mode 1: Fixed DC Mode 2: Pure Opposed Mode 3: Hybrid DC Floor (Roll vs Static Number) (Attacker vs Defender) (Attacker vs Defender AND DC) 8.1 Mode Taxonomy & Intuitive Application Rules Check Mode Core Comparison Formula When to Apply (Intuitive Trigger) Typical Action Examples Mode 1: Fixed DC max ⁡ ( Pool ) ≥ Static DC max(Pool)≥Static DC Static obstacles, environmental hazards, downtime crafting clocks, and uncontested physical/mental feats. Climbing a sheer cliff (DC 7), picking an unattended master lock (DC 8), deciphering ancient runes (DC 6), forging an iron blade (DC 5). Mode 2: Pure Opposed max ⁡ ( Attacker ) > max ⁡ ( Defender ) max(Attacker)>max(Defender) Dynamic, chaotic clashing between two active opponents where the baseline difficulty is purely the opponent's immediate effort. Melee combat strikes where the defender actively parries/evades (Combat Pool vs Parry Pool), wrestling/grappling contests, active stealth vs active searching. Mode 3: Hybrid (DC Floor) max ⁡ ( Attacker ) > max ⁡ ( Defender ) max(Attacker)>max(Defender)
AND max ⁡ ( Attacker ) ≥ DC Floor max(Attacker)≥DC Floor Complex, technical actions that carry an intrinsic physical/spatial difficulty floor, OR acting against passive obstacles actively defended. Ranged attacks at extreme distance / heavy cover (Must beat Evasion AND clear Distance DC Floor), channeling high-tier spells against target Resilience (Must beat Resilience AND clear Spell Complexity DC Floor). 8.2 Mode 3 Deep Dive (Why Hybrid DC Floors Prevent Absurdities) In a pure opposed check, if an archer shoots at a target 200 feet away (Tier 4 Extreme Distance) and the target slips on mud, rolling a 2 on Evasion, should a rolled 3 by the archer hit? No. Intuition dictates that hitting a target at 200 feet has an intrinsic ballistic spatial difficulty (e.g., Distance Floor DC 7). Even if the target rolls a 2, if the archer rolls a 5, the arrow falls short or drifts due to wind (Failed vs DC Floor 7). To hit, the archer must roll at least a 7 OR higher than the target's Evasion face (whichever is higher)! 9. The Competency Floor (Investment-Driven Mastery & Engineered Hard Caps) To give players granular control over mastery and establish engineered hard caps where grandmasters literally cannot whiff on routine checks, our system incorporates Competency Floors (Fixed Die Minimums). 9.1 Decoupling Competency Ranks from Character Level Crucially, Competency Ranks (Untrained, Trained, Expert, Master, Legendary) measure direct player investment in a specific Action Mastery Domain (Combat, Lore, Subterfuge, etc.), regardless of overall Character Level (1 to 20+). A Level 20 Archmage with zero investment in Combat Mastery (Physical weapon fighting) falls strictly under the Untrained (Rank 0) competency level when swinging a sword (2d6, Floor 0). Conversely, a Level 6 dedicated Fighter who has invested all their domain points and class feats into Combat Mastery can reach Master (Rank 3) or temporarily step into Legendary (Rank 4) during a heroic surge! When rolling a check pool, your Proficiency Tier (Untrained to Legendary) sets a guaranteed minimum floor (F) on your highest die: Final Check Result = max ⁡ ( max ⁡ ( Rolled Pool Faces ) , Competency Floor ) Final Check Result=max(max(Rolled Pool Faces),Competency Floor) 9.2 The 5 Competency Levels (Investment-Driven Step & Floor Scaling) 0. Untrained (Zero Investment at ANY Character Level): 2dX keep highest, Floor = 0 (Pure random roll) 1. Trained (Basic Professional Investment): 3dX keep highest (+1B), Floor = 3 (Guaranteed minimum face of 3) 2. Expert (Dedicated Specialization): 3dX keep highest + 1 Die Step-Up, Floor = 5 (Guaranteed minimum face of 5) 3. Master (Elite Domain Grandmastery): 4dX keep highest (+2B) + 2 Die Step-Ups, Floor = 7 (Guaranteed minimum face of 7) 4. Legendary (Mythic Domain Apex / Surge): 5dX keep highest (+3B) + 3 Die Step-Ups, Floor = 9 (Guaranteed minimum face of 9) 9.3 Engineered Mastery Guarantees (Fixed DC Checks) Because of this engineered floor, characters achieve absolute mathematical immunity to failing challenges below their competency tier without table-side arithmetic: Trained (Floor 3): Immune to failing DC 3 Routine tasks (100% success rate). Expert (Floor 5): Immune to failing DC 5 Challenging tasks (100% success rate). Master (Floor 7): Immune to failing DC 7 Formidable tasks (100% success rate). Legendary (Floor 9): Immune to failing DC 9 Heroic tasks (100% success rate). 10. Multi-Success Complex Checks (Threshold T + Required Beats S — DEC-036) To achieve smooth, fine-grained difficulty scaling without introducing numbers outside our 5 fixed DCs (2 to 12), our check engine supports Multi-Success Complex Checks. Target Difficulties can specify both a DC Threshold (T = 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) AND a Required Number of Successes (S = 1 to 4+ dice meeting/exceeding T simultaneously). 10.1 Multi-Success Resolution Mechanics When attempting a complex task (e.g., picking a masterwork clockwork lock, forging adamantine, or casting a multi-zone ritual spell): Assemble your check pool (say, 4d10 keep highest). Roll the pool and apply your Competency Floor (F) to the highest face. Count how many total dice in your pool show a value greater than or equal to the DC Threshold (T). If your count equals or exceeds the Required Successes (S), the complex task succeeds! Any extra beating dice beyond S award Special Effect Tokens ([SET]). 10.2 Finer Probability Granularity (Atomic Stepping) As proved in our mathematical simulations (sim_multi_success_granularity.py), requiring multiple successes (S = 2 or 3) allows the GM to dial in exact intermediate difficulty percentages (say, 35% vs 48% vs 58% vs 78%) without ever changing the core T threshold (say, DC 7): Level 5 Expert (3d10, Floor 5) vs DC 7: 1 beat (Standard Formidable) = 78.4%. 2 beats (Complex Formidable) = 35.2%. Level 9 Master (4d12, Floor 7) vs DC 9: 1 beat (Standard Heroic) = 80.2%. 2 beats (Complex Heroic) = 40.7%. 3 beats (Grand Heroic) = 11.1%. Pulverized Skill Matrix & Modular Class/Path Architecture

To ensure our skill system achieves maximum simulationist realism before consolidating into an actionable tabletop mechanics list, we must pulverize general capabilities into their Atomic (Pulverized) Elements, mapping them across single attributes and Physical + Mental Hybrid Linkages (STR/DEX/CON + INT/WIS/CHA).

Furthermore, we formalize our Player-Created Backgrounds (DEC-045) and our 4-to-5 Level Modular Class/Path Hybrid Architecture (DEC-047), uniting D&D 3.5e multiclassing with Shadow of the Demon Lord (SotDL) path freedom across our 20 levels.

1. Player-Created Backgrounds & Modular Class/Path Hybrid (DEC-045 & DEC-047)
1.1 Player-Created Backgrounds (DEC-045)

Rather than choosing from a restrictive list of 10 hardcoded backgrounds (e.g., Acolyte, Soldier), the player creates their own unique Background (Origin) at Level 1 by selecting two foundational elements:

One Primary Attribute Focus (STR, DEX, CON, INT, WIS, or CHA): This attribute automatically starts at d8, and steps up automatically across campaign milestones (stepping up at Levels 5, 9, 15, and 20 -> d8 -> d10 -> d12 -> d12+1 -> Apex d12+2), guaranteeing core role capability (DEC-039).
One Primary Skill Proficiency (Trained Rank, Floor 3): Chosen from any skill not restricted by Class (e.g., Blacksmithing, Diplomacy, Survival, or Sleight of Hand).
1.2 The 4-to-5 Level Modular Class/Path Hybrid (DEC-047)

Instead of a single rigid 1-to-20 linear class (e.g., Fighter 1-20), every Class—including Base Classes (Warrior, Rogue, Caster, Priest), Specialized Classes (Berserker, Paladin, Wizard, Ranger), and Master Prestige Classes (Blade Dancer, Chronomancer, Archmage)—consists of exactly 4 to 5 Levels (1 Tier Band):

text
[ 20-Level Character Build: Layering 4-Level Modular Class Bands ]
  ├── Tier 1 (Levels 1 to 4): Base Class / Novice Path (`e.g., Warrior Lvl 1-4 OR Rogue Lvl 1-4`)
  ├── Tier 2 (Levels 5 to 8): Expert Class / Prestige Path (`e.g., Berserker Lvl 1-4 OR multiclass Wizard Lvl 1-4`)
  ├── Tier 3 (Levels 9 to 12): Master Class (`e.g., Blade Dancer Lvl 1-4 OR continue Berserker`)
  ├── Tier 4 (Levels 13 to 16): Heroic Class (`e.g., Juggernaut Lvl 1-4 OR Realm Commander Lvl 1-4`)
  └── Tier 5 (Levels 17 to 20): Legendary Class (`e.g., Mythic Avatar Lvl 1-4 OR Multiversal Titan Lvl 1-4`)
Why this hybrid elevates gameplay: When a character completes a 4-level band (Tier Boundary), they can either advance into a higher-tier prestige class (just like 3.5e Prestige Classes or SotDL Expert/Master paths) OR multiclass laterally into another base class (say, a Warrior taking 4 levels of Rogue or Wizard). Every 4-level class block awards complete, self-contained Good/Okay/Bad advancement tracks (DEC-035) and unique class maneuvers (DEC-043)!

2.1 Pure Physical Linkages (STR, DEX, CON)
Strength (STR):

Goal

Idealize a new TTRPG system bridging the vast character build options, tactical depth, and content wealth of D&D 3.5e and Pathfinder 2e with a mathless core resolution engine (no table-side arithmetic or linear +/- modifiers). The system is grounded, simulationist (4 paired defenses, specific skills, no meta-currencies), supports explicit conversion procedures (from D&D 3.5e, Shadow of the Demon Lord/Weird Wizard, PF2e, Mythras/BRP, Gloomhaven), and operates across 20 character levels and 6 High Fantasy Tiers (Trained to Mythic [21+]) using our Universal Actor Schema (Race + Background + Class/Paths + Skills + Feats).

Instructions
Strictly Zero Table-Side Arithmetic (DEC-001): Action resolution compares rolled die face values (d4 to d12+) directly against static Target Numbers (DCs 2 to 12) or opposed die faces (max vs max). Never use linear numerical modifiers (no +BAB, no +Stat mod, no -4 Power Attack).
Strictly Zero Meta-Currencies (DEC-006): All heroic luck, effort, and survivability run strictly on in-world character tracks (Stamina [2xCON], Focus [WIS+INT], daily Vancian Spell Slots, and Equipment Durability Slots [1 to 4]).
Universal Nomenclature (DEC-016): Always use Die Step-Up (Up-Shift: d8 -> d10) and Die Step-Down (Down-Shift: d10 -> d8). Never use "Hyper-Shift" or "Downshift". Boons (+1B, +2B) and Banes (+1X, +2X) add or remove dice of the SAME SIZE (3d8 keep highest). Banes remove dice (1d8 single roll; +2X -> 2d8 keep lowest / Disadvantage). Max pool ceiling is 5dX.
Universal Actor Schema (DEC-011 & DEC-045): Every single actor (PCs, human NPCs, Goblins, Ogres, Dragons) is built from 5 building blocks: Race/Ancestry + Background/Origin + Class/Paths (4-5 level bands) + Skills (Specific Allocations) + Feats (Vector Traits).
Spatial Distance Tiers (DEC-031): Tier 0: Close (0-5 ft/Melee), Tier 1: Near (10-30 ft/1 Zone), Tier 2: Medium (35-60 ft/2 Zones), Tier 3: Far (65-120 ft/3 Zones), Tier 4: Distant (125-300+ ft/Artillery/Horizon). 1 Stride ([1A]) = 30 ft = exactly 1 Tier shift.
Decoupled Competency Ranks (DEC-020): Competency Ranks (0 Untrained [Floor 0], 1 Trained [+1B, Floor 3], 2 Expert [+1B, +1 Step, Floor 5], 3 Master [+2B, +2 Steps, Floor 7], 4 Legendary [+3B, +3 Steps, Floor 9]) measure specific player investment in individual skills independent of character level (1-20).
Collaborative Decision Making: Never lock in major architectural choices (such as DEC-048 skill consolidation vs 65 pulverized skills) unilaterally without explicit user confirmation. Always present exact trade-offs and let the user decide.

Yes—this is a much stronger direction. The important distinction is:

A skill represents a transferable field of competence. An activity is a concrete objective resolved by selecting the relevant skill, approach, tools, and sometimes a class or feat feature.

That keeps the skill list meaningful without turning every recognizable action into its own skill.

1. Skill, Activity, Procedure, and Maneuver
Skill

A skill is a learned domain that can be applied to many situations.

Examples:

Lockpicking is probably too narrow as a skill.
Mechanics or Thievery is broad enough to cover locks, traps, delicate mechanisms, and improvised devices.
Disguise & Impersonation is probably too procedure-specific.
Deception, Performance, and perhaps Crafting can support it depending on the method.
Sailing is broad enough to be a skill.
Rigging a sail is an activity using Sailing, possibly with Crafting or Athletics support.
Activity

An activity is an objective that may involve one or more skills.

Examples:

Activity	Primary Skill	Possible Support
Climb a wall	Athletics	Crafting for equipment
Pick a lock	Thievery/Mechanics	Lore for unusual mechanisms
Impersonate a noble	Deception	Performance, Insight, Forgery tools
Decode a rune	Lore: Runes	Languages, Arcana tradition later
Navigate a ship	Sailing	Cartography, Survival
Interrogate a prisoner	Intimidation or Insight	Medicine, Deception
Train a beast	Beast Handling	Survival, Insight
Escape bonds	Athletics or Thievery	Crafting, specific tools
Fortify a campsite	Survival	Crafting, Engineering/Lore
Negotiate a treaty	Diplomacy	Law, History, Insight
Procedure

A procedure defines how the activity works mechanically.

For example:

Pick a Lock: Roll Thievery against the lock’s static DC. If the lock is unfamiliar, trapped, magical, or under pressure, the GM may require a supporting skill, tool, or special feature.

Maneuver

A maneuver is an intentional tactical action, usually resolved through an opposed roll.

Examples:

Trip
Disarm
Shove
Grapple
Overextend
Bleed
Feint
Called Shot

These should not generally be skills. They are actions performed using an appropriate skill or combat pool.

2. Proposed Skill Architecture

I would keep the five umbrellas, but refine their names slightly.

Domain 1: Combat Mastery

Physical and technical weapon proficiency.

Heavy Blades
Light Blades
Polearms and Spears
Axes and Picks
Hammers, Maces, and Flails
Archery
Exotic Weapons
Shield Defense
Martial Arts
Notes
Finesse and Throwable should absolutely be weapon traits, not skills.
Crossbows can remain part of Archery, with Mechanical or Loading traits determining their handling.
Grappling and Wrestling should not be a separate skill. They are combat applications of Martial Arts, usually opposed against the target’s Martial Arts, Athletics, or relevant defense.
A fighter may use Heavy Blades for a sword attack, but Trip, Disarm, or Overextend remains a maneuver layered onto that attack.
Exotic Weapons should be a player-named category, but the category must be approved and internally coherent: “chain weapons,” “firearms,” “double weapons,” “whips,” and so on.

One possible concern is that nine weapon skills are already highly granular. That is acceptable if weapon specialization is meant to be a major build axis. A character should not need every weapon skill to be combat-capable, but should become distinctly better within a chosen family.

Domain 2: Athletics and Survival

Gross physical activity, endurance, wilderness competence, and movement.

Athletics
Swimming
Jumping
Riding
Survival
Sailing
Animal Handling or Beast Handling
Athletics

Athletics should cover:

Climbing
Sprinting
Forced marching
Lifting
Carrying
Balancing under physical pressure
Breaking objects
Physical escapes
Endurance challenges

Climbing and sprinting should not be separate skills. They are applications of Athletics.

Swimming

Swimming deserves to remain distinct if water environments are important in the game. It can cover:

Swimming
Diving
Treading water
Underwater endurance
Resisting currents
Jumping

Jumping can remain separate if you want a granular physical system. Otherwise, it could be folded into Athletics.

My recommendation is:

Keep Jumping separate if tactical movement and vertical environments are common.
Fold it into Athletics if you want a shorter skill list.
Survival

Survival covers:

Tracking
Foraging
Hunting
Weather reading
Finding water
Wilderness navigation
Camp defense
Camp selection
Basic fieldcraft
Riding

Riding covers control of a mount under ordinary conditions. Extreme riding activities may use a second skill:

Ride through combat: Riding + relevant Combat skill
Calm a frightened animal: Riding or Beast Handling + Insight
Cross dangerous terrain: Riding + Survival
Mounted charge: Riding + weapon skill
Sailing

I recommend making Sailing a real skill rather than an activity. It is a transferable professional domain, like medicine or blacksmithing.

It covers:

Helm and navigation at sea
Reading wind and water
Shipboard emergency response
Basic crew coordination
Sailing maneuvers
Weather judgment

However:

Rigging is an activity using Sailing or Crafting.
Ship repair uses Crafting.
Charting a route uses Cartography.
Naval combat uses Sailing plus an appropriate weapon or command skill.
Beast Handling

Beast Taming and Training should be activities within a broader skill:

Beast Handling covers understanding, controlling, calming, training, and working with animals.

Activities include:

Calm a frightened beast
Teach a command
Train a mount
Break an animal’s aggression
Identify animal behavior
Coordinate a trained animal in combat

This can use Insight for emotional reading, Survival for wild animals, and Riding for mounted control.

Domain 3: Subterfuge and Perception

Stealth, sensory awareness, tactical movement, and covert manipulation.

Moving Silently
Hide
Listen
Spot
Sleight of Hand
Thievery
Shadowing
Disguise or perhaps no separate Disguise skill
Moving Silently and Hide

These should remain separate.

Moving Silently defeats auditory detection.
Hide defeats visual detection.
A character attempting to sneak past a guard may need both, but normally only the relevant one is rolled at a time.
Listen and Spot

These should also remain separate if you want simulationist perception.

Listen detects sound, voices, movement, and hidden activity.
Spot detects visual details, concealed objects, ambushes, and movement.

“Notice something” is not a universal Perception skill. The GM identifies the relevant sense and calls for the appropriate skill.

Thievery

I strongly recommend adding Thievery as a broad skill.

It covers:

Pickpocketing
Lockpicking
Trap disarming
Concealing stolen objects
Bypassing simple security
Tampering with mechanisms
Escape artistry using tools or clever handwork

This is better than making Lockpicking and Trap Disarming independent skills.

Shadowing

I would not make Shadowing a separate skill. It is an activity using:

Moving Silently
Hide
Spot
Survival
Deception, when maintaining a cover identity

The player’s chosen method determines the skill.

Disguise and Impersonation

These should also be activities rather than a standalone skill.

Possible approaches:

Deception: maintain the false identity under questioning.
Performance: convincingly portray mannerisms, speech, and behavior.
Crafting: create the disguise, costume, or prosthetics.
Insight: study the person being impersonated.
Forgery: create supporting documents.

This produces a more interesting result than a single “Disguise” roll.

3. Domain 4: Lore and Crafting

This is where the X categories require the most structure.

I recommend dividing the umbrella into three different things:

Technical skills
Academic Lore skills
Professional Craft skills
Core skills
Anatomy and Healing
Engineering
Crafting
Cartography
Languages and Scripts
Research
Lore Specialties
Knowledge Specialties

The last two need a clear distinction.

4. Craft — X
Crafting as the general skill

Crafting is the ability to make, repair, modify, and evaluate physical objects.

It covers general competence with tools and materials, but should not make a character equally good at every trade.

A character chooses one or more Craft specialties.

Suggested Craft specialties
Armorsmithing
Weaponsmithing
Blacksmithing
Bowyer and Fletching
Leatherworking
Tailoring and Weaving
Woodworking
Stoneworking
Masonry
Carpentry
Shipwright
Engineering
Siegecraft
Alchemy
Poisoncraft
Jewelry and Gemcutting
Glassworking
Pottery and Ceramics
Cooking and Brewing
Herbalism
Clockwork and Mechanisms
Trapmaking
Forgery and Document Production
Disguise Construction
Wand, Rune, or Magical Item Crafting after the magic system is defined
Recommended rule

A character does not need a separate skill rank in every craft. Instead:

Crafting is the parent skill; each specialty is a trained field that determines what the character can make or repair.

For example:

Crafting — Blacksmithing
Crafting — Shipwright
Crafting — Alchemy

A character may be a Master Blacksmith without being competent at alchemy.

Why not make every craft a full skill?

Because that creates dozens of isolated skills that rarely matter in the same campaign. Specialties preserve granularity without requiring every craft to occupy the same character-sheet space as Archery or Diplomacy.

5. Lore — X

Lore should represent practical, cultural, traditional, or esoteric bodies of knowledge that are not necessarily academic sciences.

Suggested Lore specialties:

Ancient Civilizations
Archaeology and Ruins
Religions and Cults
Mythology
Folklore
Nobility and Heraldry
War and Military History
Guilds and Organizations
Criminal Underworld
Local Regions
Planar Realms
Monsters and Beasts
Undead
Demons and Outsiders
Fey
Dragons
Giants
Elementals
Curses and Superstitions
Runes and Sigils
Languages and Scripts
Law and Custom
Court Etiquette
Trade Routes and Markets
Piracy and Seafaring
Political Factions

Lore is what a character knows because of tradition, experience, culture, travel, or specialized study.

Examples:

Knowing that a vampire must be invited into a home: Lore — Undead
Recognizing an ancient royal seal: Lore — Heraldry
Understanding a forbidden cult’s rituals: Lore — Cults
Knowing how goblin clans negotiate: Lore — Goblins or Local Regions
6. Knowledge — X

I would reserve Knowledge for formal, analytical, or technical fields.

Suggested Knowledge specialties:

History
Geography
Mathematics
Natural Philosophy
Astronomy
Geology
Biology
Anatomy
Medicine
Chemistry
Engineering
Architecture

However, there is considerable overlap between Knowledge, Lore, and Crafting. To avoid redundant skills, I suggest this distinction:

Category	Core Question	Example
Knowledge	How does this work?	Understanding a cipher
Lore	What is known about this culture, creature, tradition, or place?	Recognizing a cult’s symbol
Crafting	Can I make, repair, or modify it?	Creating a cipher wheel
Anatomy and Healing	Can I diagnose or treat a living body?	Treating a wound
Deciphering runes and crypts

This should be a procedure, not necessarily one skill.

Possible approaches:

Languages and Scripts: translate the writing.
Lore — Runes: recognize cultural or magical symbolism.
Knowledge — Cryptography: solve a cipher.
Arcane tradition: understand magical function.
Thievery: identify a trapped or tampered inscription.

A single inscription may require one roll or several stages depending on its complexity.

7. Anatomy and Healing

This should remain a full skill because it has a coherent and important domain.

It covers:

First aid
Diagnosis
Triage
Surgery
Stabilizing wounds
Treating poison and disease
Identifying anatomy
Treating specific wound conditions

Possible specialties:

Field Medicine
Surgery
Herbal Medicine
Anatomy
Midwifery
Veterinary Medicine
Toxicology

You could treat these as specialties beneath one skill rather than separate skills.

8. Cartography and Mapmaking

I recommend making Cartography a specialty of either Knowledge or Crafting, depending on the intended use.

Reading a map: Knowledge — Geography
Creating a reliable map: Cartography
Surveying terrain: Cartography + Survival
Navigating by map: Cartography or Sailing
Forging a map: Cartography + Forgery
Identifying a map’s creator or era: Lore

My preferred structure is:

Cartography as a Knowledge/Crafting specialty, not a universal standalone skill.

It is a real field of competence, but it does not need to compete for the same space as Athletics or Diplomacy.

Performance can support impersonation, diplomacy, deception, leadership, and magical traditions later.

10. Recommended Activity Resolution Model

To prevent activities from becoming multi-roll bureaucracy, use this structure:

Standard activity

One skill roll.

Pick a lock: Thievery.

Complex activity

One primary roll, with a supporting skill changing the fictional conditions, available approaches, or consequences—not automatically adding a numerical bonus.

Impersonate a duke:

Deception is primary.
Performance establishes mannerisms.
Crafting creates the disguise.
Lore provides knowledge of court customs.
Forgery creates documents.

The character does not necessarily roll all four. The player chooses an approach, or the GM calls for stages when the activity genuinely contains separate obstacles.

Team activity

One lead character rolls; assistants contribute through preparation, tools, positioning, or a suitable assistance rule.

Class or feat interaction

Class abilities should alter what is possible:

A Rogue can attempt complex locks without specialized tools.
A Ranger can navigate wilderness without a map.
A Fighter can use Martial Arts to grapple as part of an attack.
A Courtier can use Diplomacy to establish formal negotiation rights.
A Wizard may identify magical runes through an Arcane tradition skill.

This keeps class identity meaningful without turning class features into skill replacements.

The main structural question for us is whether Craft, Lore, and Knowledge should be parent skills with specialties, or whether each specialty should be an independently ranked skill. My recommendation is parent skill plus specialty, with only the specialty fields relevant to a character appearing on the character sheet.

The comparison strongly supports your revised direction, but it also reveals several holes. The major lesson is that the four editions use three different models:

D&D 3.5e / Pathfinder 1e: long lists of individually ranked skills, with many narrow applications folded into broader skills.
D&D 5e: very compressed universal skills, with tools and backgrounds carrying much of the specialization.
Pathfinder 2e: broad core skills plus an intentionally open-ended Lore system.

Your system should probably combine:

3.5e/PF1e’s specificity,
PF2e’s clean separation between broad skills and Lore,
and 5e’s use of tools and background competence.

Strengths

3.5e is very good at representing specialized training:

A character can be excellent at Disable Device but poor at social skills.
Knowledge domains are explicitly differentiated.
Craft and Profession are open-ended.
Languages and scholarly fields are represented separately.
Tumble, Escape Artist, Use Rope, and similar skills support detailed procedures.
Weaknesses
Many skills are too narrow or repetitive.
Listen, Search, and Spot create redundant perception bookkeeping.
Balance, Climb, Jump, Swim, and Tumble can feel like separate pieces of one physical competency.
Craft and Profession are underdefined despite having excellent structural potential.
Some skills exist mainly because the game requires a place to attach a specific rule.
Skill ranks, class skill costs, cross-class costs, and ability modifiers create substantial overhead.
Lesson for your system

3.5e demonstrates that granular skill identity is valuable, but its individual skill list should not be copied directly. We should preserve the domains while converting narrow procedures into activities.

Pathfinder 1e

PF1e largely retains the 3.5e architecture, with refinements such as:

Acrobatics combining Balance and Tumble.
Perception combining Listen, Search, and Spot.

Use Magic Device remaining separate.
Profession and Craft remaining open-ended.
Escape Artist, Handle Animal, Ride, and Sleight of Hand remaining distinct.

PF1e shows how to consolidate without completely destroying specialization.

The best examples are:

Acrobatics combining Balance and Tumble.
Perception combining multiple sensory skills.
Linguistics combining language acquisition and written-language expertise.
Disable Device retaining a clear technical identity.
Weaknesses
Perception becomes an extremely dominant skill.
Acrobatics becomes overloaded.
Knowledge remains fragmented into many fields but is often difficult to adjudicate.
Craft, Profession, and Perform have a lot of conceptual overlap.
Skill investment is still heavily influenced by class-skill rules and rank economics.
Lesson for your system

PF1e is useful as a source for identifying which 3.5e skills can be combined. However, it still treats too many activities as skills.

It separates:

2. Holes in the Current List

Your current list is already structurally sound, but I see several important omissions.

Hole 1: Acrobatics, Balance, and Tumbling

Add:

Acrobatics: Balance, tumbling, controlled falls, evasive movement, and precise body control.

This is the cleanest option and follows PF1e/PF2e.

Option B: Divide the functions
Athletics: forceful movement and endurance.
Acrobatics: balance, tumbling, precision movement.

Broad approach

3. Craft, Lore, and Knowledge: Three Possible Models
Model A: Three Parent Skills with Specialties

Example:

Crafting — Blacksmithing
Crafting — Alchemy
Lore — Undead
Lore — Nobility
Knowledge — History
Knowledge — Engineering
Advantages
Very flexible.
Character sheet remains organized.
Specialties can be added without redesigning the whole system.
Excellent for high option density.
Disadvantages
The distinction between parent skill and specialty can be confusing.
It may create two layers of proficiency.
Players may ask whether “Crafting” itself can be rolled without a specialty.
Model B: Every Specialty Is an Independent Skill

Example:

Blacksmithing
Alchemy
Undead Lore
Nobility Lore
History
Engineering
Advantages
Maximum specificity.
Very clear investment.
Strong niche protection.
Closest to 3.5e’s Knowledge, Craft, and Profession model.
Disadvantages
Character sheets become crowded.
A player may have to choose among dozens of skills.
Many specialties will be campaign-dependent.
It risks recreating 3.5e’s skill bloat.
Model C: Broad Skills Plus Open-Ended Lore

Example:

Crafting is a broad skill.
Lore is individually named.
Knowledge is not a universal skill; formal knowledge is represented by Lore or a specific skill.

A character might have:

Crafting
Crafting Specialty: Blacksmithing
Lore: Undead
Lore: Imperial Law
Lore: Sailing Routes
Engineering
Anatomy and Healing
Advantages
Closest to PF2e’s most successful design.
Keeps Lore flexible and campaign-responsive.
Prevents a redundant generic Knowledge skill.
Supports both broad competence and narrow expertise.
Lets “Lore — X” become a true character-building vector.
Disadvantages
Requires clear GM guidance for selecting Lore fields.
“Lore” can become too broad if not bounded.
Crafting still needs a defined specialty procedure.
4. Recommended Result

I recommend Model C, with one adjustment:

Crafting should use defined specialties; Lore should be open-ended; Knowledge should not exist as one generic skill.
