Shared Spell-Slot Progression: Comparative Research Catalogue

Research scope: Pathfinder 2e, D&D 3.5e, 13th Age, Shadow of the Demon Lord, and D&D 5e.
Primary design question: How should our shared spell-slot pool progress across character levels and modular paths without fractional caster levels or table-side arithmetic?

This document catalogs how the reference systems answer the seven OD-001A questions. It is comparative research, not yet canonical rules.

1. OD-001A Questions
How many spell slots does a character receive at each Character Level and High Fantasy Tier?
How do class and modular path levels contribute to a shared slot pool without fractional caster levels or table-side arithmetic?
Should full, partial, limited, and noncasting paths use distinct discrete progression tracks?
When a character multiclasses, how are slot contributions combined?
Does a character's highest Tradition Rank limit the highest slot they can use?
Do advanced paths increase slot quantity, maximum Spell Rank, or both?
How does Mythic advancement expand or transform the shared slot pool?
2. Pathfinder 2e
2.1 Basic model

PF2e uses spell ranks, not traditional spell levels for most rules presentation. A spellcaster receives a number of slots at each rank they can cast. Full spellcasters typically gain access to higher ranks as they level, with the exact class table determining the progression.

Cantrips are not prepared into ordinary slots and scale automatically with the character's spellcasting progression. Focus spells use a separate Focus Point pool and are not ordinary spell slots.

PF2e has both prepared and spontaneous casters, but both ultimately use rank-based spell slots. The preparation/repertoire distinction is separate from slot capacity.

2.2 Answers to the OD-001A questions
1. How many slots by level and tier?

PF2e answers this with class-specific tables. A full caster normally gains spell slots at every available spell rank and unlocks higher ranks at specific character levels. The exact number is usually a small fixed number per rank, with class features, spellcasting benefits, and special subsystems modifying the result.

PF2e does not use our six High Fantasy Tiers as a resource framework. Its progression is level-based and rank-based.

2. How do class/path levels contribute?

A class grants its own spellcasting progression. Archetype spellcasting feats grant additional spellcasting at a deliberately slower progression. PF2e does not generally ask the table to calculate a fractional universal caster level; the archetype feat has a defined progression.

3. Full, partial, limited, and noncasters?

Yes. PF2e distinguishes full spellcasting classes, bounded or partial spellcasting options, innate spellcasting, focus spellcasting, rituals, and noncasters with magical feats. These are represented through different class or archetype features rather than one universal contribution formula.

4. Multiclassing and shared slots?

Ordinary multiclass archetypes do not simply merge all casting into one universal pool. A character may have their primary class spellcasting and a separate archetype spellcasting progression. Each source has defined access and progression.

This is highly controlled but not the cleanest model for our desired universal pool.

5. Does proficiency limit highest spell rank?

Yes, in practice. A spellcasting proficiency rank and class progression determine access to higher-rank spells. A character cannot use a high-rank slot to cast a spell they cannot access by rank or proficiency. Proficiency also affects spell attack rolls, spell DCs, and other casting checks.

6. Do advanced paths increase slots, maximum rank, or both?

They can do either. Class progression unlocks higher spell ranks and provides slots. Feats and archetypes can add spells, focus spells, spell slots, or restricted access. The system generally separates proficiency, spell rank, and slot availability.

7. Mythic advancement?

The standard PF2e level progression ends at level 20. Mythic rules and high-level subsystems are separate from ordinary spell-slot progression. Mythic power is not simply represented by adding more ordinary spell slots.

2.3 Relevant lessons
Spell rank and spell proficiency are separate but interact cleanly.
Focus Points are a useful separate resource for special magical effects.
Archetypes demonstrate how slower secondary casting can be represented without fractional caster levels.
Separate preparation and spontaneous models can coexist with rank-based slots, but multiclassing becomes more complex when each source maintains a separate progression.
Heightening is a deliberate operation; higher slots do not universally improve every spell automatically.
3. D&D 3.5e
3.1 Basic model

D&D 3.5e uses class-specific spell slots by spell level. Each class has its own progression table. A character's ability score may provide bonus spells, and some classes receive special domain, school, or specialization slots.

Caster Level is a separate class-derived value that scales spell duration, range, damage, dispelling, overcoming resistance, and other effects. Spell slots and Caster Level are related but not identical.

Different classes may use prepared spellcasting, spontaneous casting, or specialized systems. Clerics, Druids, and Wizards prepare spells; Sorcerers know a limited repertoire and cast spontaneously; Bards use a different spontaneous progression.

3.2 Answers to the OD-001A questions
1. How many slots by level and tier?

Every class has its own table. A full caster gradually gains access to spell levels 1 through 9. Partial casters gain lower levels more slowly or stop at a lower maximum. Bonus spells depend on the casting ability score. Specialist Wizards may receive an additional specialist spell slot at each spell level but lose access to prohibited schools.

D&D 3.5e has no High Fantasy Tier resource model. Its important breakpoints are class levels and spell levels.

2. How do class/path levels contribute?

They do not combine into one shared pool by default. Each class level contributes to that class's own spellcasting progression. Prestige classes can advance an existing spellcasting class, often by granting “+1 level of existing spellcasting class.”

Some prestige classes advance Caster Level, spells known, spells per day, and other class features together; others advance only selected parts.

3. Full, partial, limited, and noncasters?

Yes, but mostly through separate class tables:

Full casters reach 9th-level spells.
Partial casters reach lower maximum spell levels or progress later.
Limited casters may have small spell lists or restricted daily slots.
Noncasters have no ordinary spell-slot progression.
Some classes use separate systems such as invocations, maneuvers, psionics, or supernatural abilities.
4. Multiclassing and shared slots?

Spell slots remain separate by class. A Cleric 3/Wizard 3 has Cleric slots and Wizard slots, each using the appropriate class's preparation and spell access. Caster Level is likewise tracked separately unless a prestige class advances one of the classes.

This produces high granularity but substantial bookkeeping.

5. Does proficiency limit highest spell rank?

A class's spellcasting ability and class level determine the highest spell level available. Ability scores also gate access to spells. Skill ranks do not normally determine spell level access; Caster Level is a class progression rather than a general skill rank.

The closest lesson for our system is the distinction between:

Spell access.
Daily slots.
Caster-level scaling.
Ability-score prerequisites.
6. Do advanced paths increase slots, maximum rank, or both?

Prestige classes may advance existing spellcasting, which generally improves spells per day, spells known, maximum spell level, and Caster Level as specified. Other prestige classes grant limited casting or unique spell-like abilities.

7. Mythic advancement?

The ordinary 3.5e system ends at level 20, with epic and epic spellcasting rules handled separately. Epic progression may increase caster level and spellcasting capacity, but it is not a simple continuation of ordinary class-slot tables.

3.3 Relevant lessons
Caster Level is powerful for spell scaling, but separate caster levels become cumbersome in multiclassing.
Prestige-class “advance existing spellcasting” is a useful model for modular paths.
Independent class spell lists and pools maximize class identity but conflict with our shared Tradition model.
Bonus slots based on ability score add complexity and should probably not be copied directly.
Our proposed model can preserve 3.5e-style intrinsic spell scaling by using Tradition Competency instead of separate Caster Levels.
4. 13th Age
4.1 Basic model

13th Age does not use a universal Vancian spell-slot table in the same way as D&D 3.5e or 5e. Characters select powers, spells, talents, and class features according to class level. Abilities may be:

At-will.
Once per battle.
Recharge-based.
Daily.
Flexible or escalation-based, depending on class.

Spellcasters often have a small number of highly impactful powers rather than a large grid of slots by spell level.

4.2 Answers to the OD-001A questions
1. How many slots by level and tier?

There is no universal slot-by-rank progression. The class determines how many powers or spells the character has at each level and how often each can be used.

13th Age's level bands are more important than a spell-slot table. Characters gain new powers and replace or improve older ones as they advance.

2. How do class/path levels contribute?

The class level directly determines available powers. The system does not normally calculate a universal caster level from fractional class contributions.

3. Full, partial, limited, and noncasters?

Class design handles this directly. A Wizard, Cleric, Sorcerer, Bard, or other magical class receives its own power cadence. Noncasters receive martial or utility powers using the same broad frequency categories.

4. Multiclassing and shared slots?

13th Age is primarily class-based. Optional multiclassing combines class features or power selections, but it does not provide a standard universal spell-slot pool comparable to 5e.

5. Does proficiency limit highest spell rank?

There is generally no separate spellcasting proficiency rank equivalent to PF2e. Class level and the specific power determine whether an ability is available. Some effects scale with level or use class-based attack and defense mechanics.

6. Do advanced paths increase slots, maximum rank, or both?

New levels provide new powers, improved damage, improved effects, and sometimes replacement or upgraded versions. The system usually does not express this as increasing spell slots and maximum spell rank separately.

7. Mythic advancement?

13th Age has high-level and epic-style play but does not use a standard Mythic spell-slot transformation in its ordinary core progression. Epic or campaign-specific rules are needed beyond the standard level range.

4.3 Relevant lessons
Frequency categories can replace a large slot matrix for some abilities.
The system is excellent at making every spell or power feel impactful.
A shared pool could borrow the distinction between at-will, encounter, recharge, and daily effects, but our Vancian commitment means this should be treated as a secondary inspiration rather than the core model.
13th Age offers a useful approach to high-level spell replacement and scaling without simply adding more slots.
5. Shadow of the Demon Lord
5.1 Basic model

SotDL uses Power rather than a traditional caster level or spell-slot table. Power determines the highest rank of spell a character can cast. Paths grant traditions and individual spells.

Spells typically have their own number of castings or uses. A spell may be usable once, twice, or several times per day depending on its entry. The character does not spend a generic slot of the spell's rank in the D&D sense.

Traditions are modular and can be acquired through Novice, Expert, and Master paths. A character can combine traditions from multiple paths.

5.2 Answers to the OD-001A questions
1. How many slots by level and tier?

There is no shared spell-slot pool. Power increases with character advancement and determines the highest spell rank available. Each individual spell specifies its number of castings.

SotDL's path bands correspond conceptually to our modular path bands, but the system uses Power and per-spell castings rather than universal slots.

2. How do class/path levels contribute?

Paths grant Power increases, traditions, talents, and spells. There is no fractional caster-level calculation. A character's accumulated Power is a bounded progression supplied by ancestry, novice/expert/master paths, and level advancement.

3. Full, partial, limited, and noncasters?

Yes, through path design. A caster-focused path grants more Power, traditions, and spells. A martial path may grant no Power or only a limited magical feature. Hybrid paths grant smaller or more restricted access.

4. Multiclassing and shared slots?

There are no shared slots to combine. A character accumulates Power, traditions, and spells from their paths. Multiple paths can broaden the character's magical repertoire, while the Power value controls the highest spell rank.

5. Does proficiency limit highest spell rank?

Power determines the highest spell rank. There is no separate Tradition Competency Rank equivalent to our skill model. Traditions determine spell access; Power determines spell rank capacity.

This is the clearest precedent for separating:

Tradition access.
Spell-rank capacity.
Individual spell acquisition.
6. Do advanced paths increase slots, maximum rank, or both?

Advanced paths primarily increase Power, grant higher-rank spells, add traditions, and provide talents. They do not increase a universal slot pool because slots are not the core resource model.

7. Mythic advancement?

SotDL's standard progression is ten levels and does not have our six-tier Mythic structure. Beyond-standard advancement requires separate campaign or supplement rules.

5.3 Relevant lessons
Power is a clean bounded measure of maximum spell rank.
Individual per-spell castings give designers precise control over strong effects.
Modular paths can grant access without creating separate class spell lists.
The system is an excellent model for Tradition access but not a direct model for our committed shared Vancian slots.
We can borrow its discrete full/partial/limited path contribution concept without copying its per-spell-use model.
6. D&D 5e
6.1 Basic model

D&D 5e uses a shared spell-slot progression for multiclass characters with ordinary spellcasting. Each class still has its own spell list and preparation or known-spell rules, but spell slots are combined through a multiclass spellcaster-level table.

Full casters contribute one level per class level. Half-casters and third-casters contribute fractions according to class rules, usually rounded down. Warlock Pact Magic is separate and does not combine normally with ordinary spellcasting slots.

Cantrips are at-will and scale primarily from total character level. Higher-level slots can be used to cast lower-level spells, and many spells improve when cast with a higher slot.

6.2 Answers to the OD-001A questions
1. How many slots by level and tier?

The standard multiclass spellcaster table provides a shared number of slots by spell level based on the combined spellcaster level. Full casters progress from 1st-level slots at low level to 9th-level slots at high level. Slot quantity increases at defined character-level breakpoints.

D&D 5e has no formal High Fantasy Tier resource structure, though its spell-level breakpoints create practical tiers of play.

2. How do class/path levels contribute?

Class levels contribute to a combined spellcaster level:

Full-caster levels contribute fully.
Half-caster levels contribute partially.
Third-caster levels contribute more slowly.
The final result is checked against one shared slot table.

This is mathematically compact in the book but requires fractional progression and rounding rules during character creation.

3. Full, partial, limited, and noncasters?

Yes. Full, half, and third casters use different contribution rates. Warlock Pact Magic is a distinct casting system. Racial spells, feats, and innate magic operate outside the ordinary class slot progression.

4. Multiclassing and shared slots?

Ordinary spellcaster levels combine into one shared slot pool. However, spells known and prepared remain class-specific. A multiclass Wizard/Cleric has one shared pool but separately tracks Wizard and Cleric spell access and preparation.

This is the closest direct precedent for our desired shared-slot model, but our proposal goes further by making Tradition lists shared rather than class-owned.

5. Does proficiency limit highest spell rank?

Spellcasting class level determines which spell levels the character can learn or prepare. Proficiency bonus affects some spell attacks and class features but does not independently determine spell-slot rank.

D&D 5e's caster-level function is split between:

Class spellcasting progression.
Spell-slot table.
Ability score.
Proficiency bonus.
Character level for cantrip scaling.
6. Do advanced paths increase slots, maximum rank, or both?

Multiclass spellcaster progression increases both as the combined spellcaster level rises. Subclasses generally modify spell access and class features rather than creating a new universal slot table. Feats may add spells or limited casting without advancing ordinary spellcaster level.

7. Mythic advancement?

The standard game ends at level 20 and normally caps ordinary spell slots at 9th level. Epic boons and high-level features provide additional power but do not normally create 10th-level spell slots in the core progression.

6.3 Relevant lessons
One shared slot pool is compatible with different classes, but class-owned spell lists create the exact shared-Tradition ambiguity we are removing.
The combined spellcaster-level table is familiar but uses fractions and rounding.
Separate Pact Magic demonstrates that not every supernatural resource must join the shared slot pool.
Cantrips scaling by character level is a useful precedent, though our design currently favors Essence for 0th-rank effects.
D&D 5e supports shared slots but still has class-specific preparation and acquisition, whereas our system will unify those around Traditions plus class acquisition features.
7. Comparative Matrix
System	Core resource	Spell access	Slot combination	Maximum spell rank controlled by	Multiclass complexity
Pathfinder 2e	Rank-based slots plus Focus Points	Class, archetype, spell list	Usually separate defined progressions	Class progression and spell proficiency	Medium to high
D&D 3.5e	Class-specific slots plus bonus slots	Class spell list	Separate by class	Class level, ability score, Caster Level	Very high
13th Age	At-will, battle, recharge, daily powers	Class powers	Not a universal slot system	Class level and power design	Low to medium
Shadow of the Demon Lord	Power plus per-spell castings	Traditions and paths	No universal slots	Power	Low
D&D 5e	Shared ordinary slots; Pact Magic separate	Class spell lists	Combined multiclass caster level	Class spellcasting progression	Medium
Our system	Shared Vancian slots plus Essence	Fixed Tradition lists	Shared directly	Tradition Competency plus slot rank	Intended medium, no fractions
8. Design Conclusions for Our System

The reference systems suggest that our system should preserve the following:

PF2e: Separate spell rank from casting proficiency.
D&D 3.5e: Let casting competence scale the intrinsic effect of a spell.
13th Age: Keep individual magical effects impactful and use discrete advancement breakpoints.
SotDL: Let modular paths grant Traditions and use discrete path-based magical progression.
D&D 5e: Use one shared slot pool for multiclass spellcasters.

The main feature to avoid is D&D 5e's fractional multiclass caster-level arithmetic. Our implementation should use discrete path tags or contribution bands such as:

Full Casting.
Partial Casting.
Limited Casting.
No Casting.

The final shared-slot table should convert those path contributions into a discrete result at level-up rather than requiring players to add fractions at the table.

9. Open Questions After Comparative Research

The comparative survey does not yet answer our design choices. It narrows them to:

Should Tradition Competency alone gate the highest Spell Rank, or must a separate class/path spell-capacity track also gate it?
Should slot quantity be determined by total Character Level, cumulative casting-path bands, or a discrete full/partial/limited track?
Should higher-rank slots ever heighten lower-rank spells, or should our D&D 3.5e-style intrinsic scaling remain primary?
Should each spell have a fixed slot cost equal to its Spell Rank, or can specific spells have exceptional slot costs?
Should 0th-rank spells be entirely Essence-based, entirely at-will, or divided into both categories?
How much spell-slot growth should occur at Levels 1, 5, 9, 13, 17, and Mythic advancement?

Based on this analysis, how would you answer the OD-001A questions?

OD-001A Questions

How many spell slots does a character receive at each Character Level and High Fantasy Tier?

How do class and modular path levels contribute to a shared slot pool without fractional caster levels or table-side arithmetic?

Should full, partial, limited, and noncasting paths use distinct discrete progression tracks?

When a character multiclasses, how are slot contributions combined?

Does a character's highest Tradition Rank limit the highest slot they can use?

Do advanced paths increase slot quantity, maximum Spell Rank, or both?

How does Mythic advancement expand or transform the shared slot pool?

Based on the comparison, I would answer OD-001A with a five-rank shared Vancian progression, using Tradition Rank as the spell-quality/access gate and class/path casting tracks as the source of daily slot volume.

Recommended OD-001A Answers
1. How many spell slots does a character receive at each Character Level and High Fantasy Tier?

I recommend five ordinary Spell Ranks aligned to the five mortal High Fantasy Tiers:

Spell Rank	High Fantasy Tier	Typical Availability
Novice	Trained	Levels 1–4
Expert	Veteran	Levels 5–8
Master	Master	Levels 9–12
Heroic	Hero	Levels 13–16
Legendary	Legend	Levels 17–20
Mythic	Mythic	Level 21+

A full caster’s baseline slot progression could be:

Level	Novice	Expert	Master	Heroic	Legendary
1	2	—	—	—	—
2	3	—	—	—	—
3	4	—	—	—	—
4	4	—	—	—	—
5	3	2	—	—	—
6	3	3	—	—	—
7	4	3	—	—	—
8	4	4	—	—	—
9	3	3	2	—	—
10	3	3	3	—	—
11	4	3	3	—	—
12	4	4	3	—	—
13	3	3	3	2	—
14	3	3	3	3	—
15	4	3	3	3	—
16	4	4	3	3	—
17	3	3	3	3	2
18	3	3	3	3	3
19	4	3	3	3	3
20	4	4	3	3	3

This provides:

More slots as the character advances.
A new maximum Spell Rank at each major tier boundary.
A recognizable D&D-style progression.
A manageable five-column table.
No need for ninth-level spell slots before the Mythic tier.

This table should be regarded as a full-caster baseline, not a final balance result. We would still need to test whether five ranks provide enough differentiation between levels inside each tier.

Cantrips and 0th-rank spells

I recommend that 0th-rank spells do not use these slots.

They use Essence instead.

text
0th-Rank Spell:
  Costs Essence.
  Does not consume a daily Spell Slot.

That gives spellcasters reliable minor magic while preserving slots for meaningful daily choices.

2. How do class and modular path levels contribute without fractional caster levels?

Use discrete Spellcasting Track contributions, not caster-level fractions.

Each class or modular path has a casting track:

Full Casting
Partial Casting
Limited Casting
No Casting

A path’s casting track provides specific rank-based progression at its own level-band boundaries.

For example:

Full Casting Path
text
Path Band 1:
  Grants Novice slot progression.

Path Band 2:
  Grants Expert slot progression.

Path Band 3:
  Grants Master slot progression.

Path Band 4:
  Grants Heroic slot progression.

Path Band 5:
  Grants Legendary slot progression.
Partial Casting Path
text
Path Band 1:
  Grants Novice access or a small Novice slot package.

Path Band 2:
  Improves Novice slots or grants limited Expert access.

Path Band 3:
  Grants stronger Novice and Expert capacity.

Path Band 4:
  Grants limited Master capacity.

Path Band 5:
  Remains below full-caster progression.
Limited Casting Path

A limited path may grant:

A small number of Novice slots.
A restricted Tradition.
A few class-granted spells.
Essence-based supernatural abilities.
No progression beyond Expert or Master unless a later path expands it.

The character sheet records the resulting slot package directly. The player does not calculate:

text
Wizard 3 + Cleric 2 + half-caster fraction + prestige fraction

Instead, each path grants discrete advancement entries.

3. Should full, partial, limited, and noncasting paths use distinct tracks?

Yes.

They should use distinct discrete tracks rather than one universal formula.

Full Casting
Access to all five ordinary Spell Ranks.
Highest slot rank advances at the major tier boundaries.
Receives the largest daily slot pool.
Typical examples: Wizard, Cleric, Nature caster, dedicated magical paths.
Partial Casting
Receives fewer slots.
Reaches higher ranks later.
May stop at Master or Heroic without a prestige path.
Typical examples: Paladin, Ranger, War Mage, Arcane Warrior.
Limited Casting
Receives a small number of slots.
Has restricted Tradition access.
Often relies on Essence, class features, weapons, or specific spells.
Typical examples: Eldritch Knight-style paths, magical rogues, specialized prestige paths.
Noncasting
Receives no ordinary daily spell slots.
May still use Essence for supernatural feats, martial techniques, ancestry powers, or psionic effects.
Can gain limited spell access through feats, items, rituals, or later paths.

This also allows “noncaster” to mean “no Vancian casting” rather than “no supernatural ability.”

4. When a character multiclasses, how are slot contributions combined?

I recommend discrete slot-package combination, not fractional caster levels.

Each path grants a recorded package:

text
Full Path Band:
  Full contribution.

Partial Path Band:
  Partial contribution.

Limited Path Band:
  Limited contribution.

At character advancement, the character’s total casting result is determined by a progression matrix.

The important rule is:

Multiclassing can broaden access and acquisition, but it should not allow a one-level dip to provide a full new tier of spell capacity.

Recommended combination priority
A full-casting path advances the primary shared slot progression.
Additional full-casting paths may broaden Traditions and acquisition, but do not duplicate the full slot package at the same level.
Partial paths contribute only when the character lacks equivalent full-casting progression.
Limited paths add narrow slot packages, Essence features, or specific spell access.
Multiple partial paths can eventually combine into a stronger progression, but only at defined discrete thresholds.

This produces three possible multiclass results:

Full caster plus noncaster
text
Wizard 4 / Fighter 4
Retains the Wizard’s full casting progression.
Gains Fighter features.
Does not gain additional slots from Fighter.
May gain martial use of Essence through Fighter feats or paths.
Full caster plus partial caster
text
Wizard 4 / Paladin 4
Wizard provides the main full-casting progression.
Paladin broadens Divine, Life, War, or Guardian access.
Paladin may provide limited additional acquisition or Essence abilities.
Paladin does not double the slot pool.
Partial caster plus partial caster
text
Paladin 4 / Ranger 4
Each contributes a partial casting package.
A combination matrix determines whether they remain Limited, become Partial, or reach a new slot threshold.
The result is recorded directly on the sheet.

This last case needs playtesting, but it is preferable to adding fractions.

5. Does highest Tradition Rank limit the highest slot a character can use?

Yes.

A character must satisfy both:

The Spell Slot requirement.
The Tradition Rank requirement.

Recommended gate:

Tradition Rank	Highest Spell Rank
Untrained	None
Trained	Novice
Expert	Expert
Master	Master
Legendary	Heroic and Legendary, subject to final Mythic rules

Example:

text
Death: Expert
Available Slots: Novice and Expert

The character can cast Expert Death spells.

text
Death: Trained
Available Slots: Novice and Expert

The character can only cast Novice Death spells.

text
Death: Expert
Available Slots: Novice only

The character understands Expert Death magic but cannot currently cast it.

This preserves the distinction between:

Magical competence.
Daily magical volume.
Spell knowledge.
Spell access.
What happens to higher slots?

A character may retain higher-rank slots even if they currently lack a sufficiently ranked Tradition. Those slots can be:

Used with another sufficiently ranked Tradition.
Used for metamagic, if permitted.
Used for future advancement.
Converted into a special ritual or Essence effect, if a rule permits.
6. Do advanced paths increase slot quantity, maximum Spell Rank, or both?

They can increase either, but they should not automatically increase both.

This gives advanced paths meaningful specialization.

Capacity Paths

Increase:

Number of slots.
Maximum usable Spell Rank.
Spell acquisition volume.

These are appropriate for:

Archmage.
High Priest.
Master Druid.
Legendary Thaumaturge.
Tradition Paths

Increase:

Tradition Rank.
Tradition access.
Spell list breadth.
Tradition feats.
Spell scaling.

These may grant few or no additional slots.

Examples:

text
Death Adept:
  Increases Death to Master.
  Adds Death spells.
  Grants necromantic feats.
  Does not increase total slots.

Archmage:
  Adds an Expert slot.
  Unlocks Master and Heroic slots.
  Does not necessarily improve Death, Rune, or Elemental rank.
Hybrid Paths

Increase:

One Tradition Rank.
A small number of slots.
A specific spell acquisition method.
A limited maximum Spell Rank.

This allows prestige classes to have distinct identities without all of them becoming “more caster level.”

7. How does Mythic advancement expand or transform the shared slot pool?

Mythic advancement should not simply add an endless number of ordinary Legendary slots.

That would encourage spell-slot inflation rather than mythic transformation.

I recommend that Mythic introduces a sixth category:

Mythic Spell Rank

Mythic spells should be:

Rare.
Expensive.
Often ritualized.
World-scale or divine in consequence.
Limited by Essence, preparation, components, locations, or narrative conditions.
Not merely stronger combat spells.
Mythic slot model

At the beginning of Mythic advancement:

text
Mythic Slots: 1

Further Mythic development may grant:

Additional Mythic slots.
A Mythic reserve that can empower lower-rank spells.
A unique Mythic signature spell.
A permanent magical domain.
A once-per-campaign or once-per-arc effect.
Access to Creation, Time, Space, Order, or Chaos.

However, we should not introduce a meta-currency. Mythic resources must remain in-world:

Essence.
Divine authority.
Bound relics.
Cosmic vows.
Mythic reagents.
Permanent transformation.
Domain control.
Long rituals.
Mythic spell scaling

At Mythic, the distinction between slot rank and Tradition Competency becomes even more important:

text
Legendary Death + Mythic Slot:
  Mythic-scale Death effect.

Legendary Death + Legendary Slot:
  Legendary-scale Death effect.

Expert Death + Mythic Slot:
  Cannot cast a Mythic Death spell.

A higher slot cannot substitute for insufficient Tradition Competency.

Recommended OD-001A Resolution
Core answers
Use five ordinary Spell Ranks aligned with the five mortal High Fantasy Tiers.
Use one shared spell-slot pool.
Give full, partial, limited, and noncasting paths separate discrete tracks.
Combine multiclassing through discrete slot packages and a progression matrix, not fractional caster levels.
Require both sufficient Tradition Rank and an appropriate Spell Slot.
Let advanced paths increase slot quantity, maximum Spell Rank, Tradition Rank, spell acquisition, or a focused combination of these.
Introduce Mythic Slots at Level 21+ rather than endlessly expanding Legendary slots.
Use Essence for 0th-rank spells, metamagic, casting stability, and supernatural features.
Keep intrinsic spell scaling tied to Tradition Competency.
Do not make higher-rank slots automatically improve lower-rank spells.
Remaining implementation tasks

The main remaining OD-001A work is now:

Finalize whether the five ordinary Spell Ranks should be called Novice, Expert, Master, Heroic, and Legendary.
Build the exact Full, Partial, Limited, and Noncasting slot tables.
Build the discrete multiclass combination matrix.
Test whether the proposed full-caster slot volume produces the desired daily resource pressure.
Determine how partial-plus-partial casting combines.
Determine whether spell slots are restored by a long camp only or through additional in-world recovery methods.
Design Mythic Slots and Mythic spell access.

2. The Simplest Version: Highest Track Wins

The simplest combination rule would be:

Use the strongest casting package the character possesses. Other casting paths grant Traditions, spells, acquisition features, and magical class abilities, but do not duplicate the main slot pool.

The Fighter levels provide martial features but no spell slots.

text

  Full Novice package

Paladin Band 1:
  Partial Novice package

Final result:
  Full Novice package
  Plus perhaps one defined Paladin support slot or Essence feature

The Paladin does not double the character’s slots merely because both classes provide magic.

This is extremely easy to run, but it makes secondary casting paths contribute very little to daily spell volume.

3. A More Flexible Version: Package Combination Matrix

To make secondary casting matter, we can use a discrete combination matrix.

9. What Does “Without Arithmetic” Mean Here?

There are two different kinds of arithmetic to distinguish.

Character-building arithmetic

At level-up, the player may need to determine their new slot package.

That can be handled through:

A progression table.
A character-builder worksheet.
A class/path combination chart.
A precomputed character sheet.

This is acceptable because it is not repeated during ordinary action resolution.

Table-side arithmetic

During play, the player should not calculate:

text
3 Wizard levels + 2 Cleric levels + half Paladin level

Instead, the character sheet should simply say:

text

or list the actual slots:

text

11. Is This Better Than a Shared Spellcasting Track?

There is an even simpler alternative:

Every character has one Spellcasting Track determined by their strongest casting path. Secondary casting paths never modify slot quantity; they only add access, spells, and class features.

This is easier to balance and resembles how many multiclass systems prevent spell-slot inflation.

The trade-off is:

Cleaner balance.
Less reward for combining two caster classes.
More emphasis on Tradition breadth and acquisition mechanics.
12. My Current Recommendation

I would use a two-layer approach:

Primary Casting Package

The strongest class/path contribution determines the character’s baseline shared slots.

text
Full > Partial > Limited > None
Secondary Casting Package

Secondary casting paths may grant a predefined support benefit:

A small number of additional slots.
Earlier access to a lower Spell Rank.
More prepared spells.
Additional Tradition access.
More Essence.
A unique acquisition method.
A special casting feature.

This is safer than allowing every class to add directly to the slot pool.

So:

text
Wizard 4 / Cleric 4:
  Full baseline
  Cleric support package

Wizard 4 / Fighter 4:
  Full baseline
  Fighter supernatural support package, if any

Paladin 4 / Ranger 4:
  Partial baseline
  Secondary partial support package
13. The Actual Concept in One Sentence

The idea is:

A class or path grants a named casting package at discrete advancement points; the strongest package establishes the shared slot baseline, and secondary casting packages modify that baseline only through explicit capped benefits—not fractional caster levels.

This is probably the safest starting point for playtesting because it prevents multiclass spell-slot explosions while still allowing secondary classes to matter through Traditions, acquisition, Essence, and class features.

D&D 5e separates:

2. Shadow of the Demon Lord: Power

SotDL does not use shared spell slots.

Instead, a character has Power, which determines the highest spell rank they can cast.

Which traditions they can access.

A character might have:

  Arcana

  Fire

Strengths for our system
Extremely simple multiclassing.

No fractional caster levels.

Very compatible with SotDL-style Tradition access.
Weaknesses for our system
It is not Vancian slot casting.
Every spell needs its own casting-use value.
A powerful spell may have one casting while a weaker spell has three, creating a lot of individual spell bookkeeping.
It does not naturally support the D&D 3.5e model where spells improve with caster level while higher-level slots do not automatically improve them.

It may make spells feel more like individual class powers than entries in a prepared spell system.
3. Why the Two Systems Feel Simpler

They simplify different problems.

D&D 5e simplifies quantity

The central question is:

How many slots do I have today?

The answer comes from one shared table.

SotDL simplifies maximum power

The central question is:

What is the highest rank of spell I can cast?

The answer comes from Power.

Our system currently wants both:

text
What is the highest Spell Rank I can cast?
  Tradition Competency.

How many spells can I cast today?
  Shared Vancian slots.

That is not inherently too complicated. It is only complicated if we add a third independent caster statistic.

I would now answer OD-001A this way:

Use a D&D 5e-style shared slot pool, with discrete class/path contributions and a single multiclass spellcasting table. Primary-track rule

The character uses the best Spellcasting Progression they possess:

Mediocre and Bad classes do not add slots automatically.
They may still add Traditions, spells, Essence features, and acquisition methods.

I agree with your decision:

Tradition Rank does not limit the highest slot a character can use.

It limits spell access and scaling, not slot access.

Example:

  Arcane: Expert
  Death: Trained

They may use those slots to cast:

Expert Arcane spells.
Trained Death spells.
Other spells from sufficiently ranked Traditions.

They cannot cast Master Death spells because Death is only Trained.

Why this is acceptable

It creates an intentional build distinction:

text

  Large daily resource pool.

High Tradition Rank:
  High-quality, high-scaling spells.

Broad Tradition investment:
  Many types of spells.

Focused Tradition investment:
  Deep scaling in one magical field.

Cleric:
  Advances Spellcasting every level.

Paladin:
  Advances Spellcasting every 2 class levels.

Eldritch Knight:
  Advances Spellcasting every 3 class levels.

Fighter:
  Does not advance Spellcasting.

The character records completed Spellcasting advancements. The total determines the character’s Spellcasting Progression Level.

For example:

text
Wizard 4:
  4 Spellcasting advancements.
  Spellcasting Progression Level 4.

Paladin 4:
  2 Spellcasting advancements.
  Spellcasting Progression Level 2.

Eldritch Knight 3:
  1 Spellcasting advancement.
  Spellcasting Progression Level 1.

The character then reads the appropriate row of the shared spell-slot table.

This is conceptually similar to SotDL’s Power, except that our progression value determines the character’s position on the slot table, rather than directly determining only the highest Spell Rank.

The calculation occurs during character advancement, not during ordinary play.

3. Should full, partial, limited, and noncasting paths use distinct discrete progression tracks?

There are no formal player-facing “Good,” “Mediocre,” or “Bad” tracks.

Those terms are design guidelines used to describe advancement cadence:

Full/reference caster: advances every class level.
Partial caster: advances every two class levels.
Limited caster: advances every three class levels or another restricted cadence.
Noncaster: does not advance Spellcasting.

Each class provides its actual advancement schedule directly.

This avoids requiring players to understand abstract fractions such as:

text
+1 caster level
+1/2 caster level
+1/3 caster level
4. When a character multiclasses, how are slot contributions combined?

Each class contributes Spellcasting advancements according to its own cadence.

The contributions are added to one shared Spellcasting Progression Level.

Examples:

text
Wizard 4 / Fighter 4:
  Wizard: 4 advancements
  Fighter: 0 advancements
  Total: Spellcasting Progression Level 4
text
Wizard 4 / Paladin 4:
  Wizard: 4 advancements
  Paladin: 2 advancements
  Total: Spellcasting Progression Level 6
text
Wizard 4 / Eldritch Knight 3:
  Wizard: 4 advancements
  Eldritch Knight: 1 advancement
  Total: Spellcasting Progression Level 5
text
Wizard 4 / Cleric 4:
  Wizard: 4 advancements
  Cleric: 4 advancements
  Total: Spellcasting Progression Level 8

All classes and Prestige Classes use the same rule. Prestige Classes differ from Base Classes through prerequisites, not through a separate multiclassing procedure.

The character has one shared slot pool determined by the final Spellcasting Progression Level.

5. Does a character’s highest Tradition Rank limit the highest slot they can use?

No.

Spellcasting Progression determines the character’s available daily spell slots.

Tradition Skills determine:

Which Tradition spells the character can access.
Which spells the character can learn or prepare.
The intrinsic scaling of those spells.
Their casting proficiency and Competency Floor.

A character may possess a high Spellcasting Progression Level while having shallow investment in a particular Tradition.

Example:

text
Spellcasting Progression Level: 10
Death: Trained
Arcane: Expert

The character receives the complete Progression Level 10 slot pool, but:

Can use only Trained-scale Death spells.
Can use Expert-scale Arcane spells.
Cannot access Death spells requiring deeper Tradition mastery.
May use higher-circle slots to cast lower-circle spells, subject to the spell rules.

This is intentional. Spellcasting capacity and Tradition mastery are separate vectors.

6. Do advanced classes and Prestige Classes increase slot quantity, maximum Spell Rank, or both?

A class or Prestige Class may provide any combination of:

Spellcasting advancements.
Tradition Skill access.
Tradition Skill advancement.
Spell acquisition.
Essence features.
Metamagic.
Special spell permissions.
Access to advanced or restricted Traditions.

Spellcasting advancement increases the character’s position on the shared slot table. It does not automatically increase Tradition mastery.

A Prestige Class may therefore specialize in:

text
Advancing Spellcasting.

or:

text
Advancing Death Tradition.

or:

text
Granting Time Tradition access.

or:

text
Providing Essence and metamagic features.

These do not need to advance together.

The class entry should state its Spellcasting Advancement cadence explicitly.

7. How does Mythic advancement expand or transform the shared slot pool?

Mythic advancement does not automatically add new ordinary spell slots beyond the Level 20 table.

Instead, Mythic advancement grants access to:

Epic Traditions.
Epic Spells.
Mythic spell effects.
Mythic versions of existing Traditions.
Cosmic or divine magical permissions.
Special uses for existing high-circle slots.

Epic Spells use the character’s existing shared Spell Slots, subject to their requirements.

For example:

text
Epic Creation Spell:
  Requires access to the Creation Tradition.
  Requires Legendary or Mythic Tradition Competency.
  Consumes a 7th-, 8th-, or 9th-circle slot.
  May also require Essence, a ritual, or a unique component.

Mythic advancement expands what magic can be done, not merely how many ordinary slots the character receives.

Consolidated Design Summary
1. Spellcasting Progression Level

Every character has a derived value called Spellcasting Progression Level.

This value determines the character’s position on the shared daily Spell Slot table.

It is separate from:

Character Level.
High Fantasy Tier.
Tradition Competency.

Ability scores.

text

Character Level 2  → Spellcasting Progression Level 2
Character Level 3  → Spellcasting Progression Level 3

Important Correction to the Proposed Mediocre Table

Under the rule:

“Advance through the Reference Spell Slot Progression table every other class level,”

a character with 20 levels in a Mediocre-casting class reaches Progression Level 10, not Progression Level 11.

Therefore, they would use the Reference Progression Level 10 row:

text
5 first-circle
4 second-circle
3 third-circle
3 fourth-circle
2 fifth-circle

They would not yet have sixth-circle slots.

To reach sixth-circle slots, the character must reach Reference Progression Level 11.

So the pure rates produce:

Advancement Rate	Progression Level at Class Level 20	Highest Circle
Full: every level	20	9th
Mediocre: every 2 levels	10	5th
Bad: every 4 levels	5	3rd

This is the mathematically consistent result using the current Reference table.

If we specifically want:

text
Full: 9th-circle maximum
Mediocre: 6th-circle maximum
Bad: 3rd-circle maximum

then Mediocre cannot simply be “every other level” unless it receives an additional advancement somewhere.

Possible solutions include:

Give Mediocre classes one extra Spell Slot Advancement at Level 1.
Give Mediocre classes one extra advancement at a later class level.
Make the Mediocre cadence +1 at levels 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, ..., 20.
Accept that pure Mediocre progression ends at 5th Circle.
Use a separate class feature to grant sixth-circle access without changing the slot progression.

My preferred solution is probably Option 4 unless playtesting indicates that sixth-circle access is necessary. It keeps the advancement cadence mathematically clean.

Important Correction to the Proposed Bad Table

The Bad table as written also appears to be an independent slot table rather than a direct reading of the Reference Spell Slot Progression table.

If Bad classes advance once every four class levels, then their slot results should be:

Class Level	Progression Level	Reference Slot Row
1–4	1	4 first-circle
5–8	2	4 first-circle
9–12	3	4 first-circle, 2 second-circle
13–16	4	4 first-circle, 2 second-circle
17–20	5	5 first-circle, 2 second-circle, 2 third-circle

That is the direct consequence of moving through the Reference table once per four class levels.

So a pure Bad caster at Class Level 20 would have:

text
5 first-circle slots
2 second-circle slots
2 third-circle slots

not the much larger slot values in the proposed Bad table.

If the larger Bad table is intentional, then it represents a separate slot-volume table, not simply a slower advancement through the Reference progression.

Yes—I agree with the design concern.

A Spell Slot Advancement should produce a visible change whenever possible. If the player gains an advancement but the table row is identical to the previous row, the advancement feels invisible and creates exactly the confusion you describe.

Important Clarification

Your Mediocre and Bad tables are not independent rules systems. They are derived from the Good/Reference table by applying a slower advancement cadence:

text
Full:
  Uses the next Reference row every class level.

Mediocre:
  Uses the next Reference row every 2 class levels.

Bad:
  Uses the next Reference row every 4 class levels.

For example:

text
Mediocre Level 10:
  Five Spell Slot Advancements.
  Uses Reference Progression Level 5.

Bad Level 16:
  Four Spell Slot Advancements.
  Uses Reference Progression Level 4.

That means the Good/Reference table is the critical table. If two adjacent Reference rows are identical, every class that advances into the second row gets no visible benefit.

The “No Invisible Advancement” Principle

I recommend adding this design requirement:

Every Reference Spell Slot Progression Level should differ meaningfully from the previous level.

A difference can be:

A new Spell Circle becoming available.
An additional slot at an existing Circle.
An increase in lower-Circle slot volume.
A new slot flexibility rule, if we eventually use one.

For the basic table, the cleanest version is:

Every advancement should either add a slot or unlock a new Spell Circle.

Current Problematic Repetitions

In the current Good table:

text
Progression Level 1:
  4 first-circle slots

Progression Level 2:
  4 first-circle slots

No change occurs.

Likewise:

text
Progression Level 3:
  4 first-circle, 2 second-circle

Progression Level 4:
  4 first-circle, 2 second-circle

Again, no change occurs.

This has amplified consequences:

Full caster

The full caster receives no new slot benefit at Progression Levels 2 and 4.

Mediocre caster

The same issue appears at the corresponding character levels after applying the slower cadence.

Bad caster

The problem becomes more noticeable because the class advances less frequently. A Bad caster may wait four levels for an advancement and then discover that the new table row is identical.

Recommended Adjustment

I would revise the Reference table so that Progression Levels 1–20 are all distinct.

The revision does not necessarily require dramatically increasing total spell slots. We can redistribute increases across the existing slot columns.

For example, instead of:

text
Level 1: 4
Level 2: 4
Level 3: 4 / 2
Level 4: 4 / 2

we might use a pattern such as:

text
Level 1: 4
Level 2: 5
Level 3: 5 / 2
Level 4: 5 / 3

However, that specific version would need to be tested against the rest of the table. We should not simply add slots without recalibrating the total daily spell volume.

The revision criteria should be:

Every row changes from the previous row.
Slot quantities never decrease.
Spell Circle unlocks remain at the intended progression points.
Full casters still reach 9th Circle at Progression Level 17.
Mediocre casters still reach 5th Circle at Character Level 17 and do not reach 6th Circle by Level 20 under the pure every-other-level cadence.
Bad casters still reach 3rd Circle at Character Level 17 under the every-four-level cadence.
The total daily spell volume remains within the intended resource budget.

The terminology you approved works well:

Project Vault: Idealized Mathless Simulationist TTRPG System

Project Vault: Idealized Mathless Simulationist TTRPG System

This workspace develops a high-option-density, simulationist fantasy TTRPG that combines:

D&D 3.5e’s class depth, feats, prestige classes, spell volume, and conversion wealth.
Pathfinder 2e’s structured progression, traits, and tactical three-action economy.
Mythras/BRP’s opposed combat, differential success, hit locations, wounds, and underlings.
Shadow of the Demon Lord / Weird Wizard’s modular class design and Tradition inspiration.
Gloomhaven-style tactical pacing and enemy management.

The system’s core constraint is zero table-side arithmetic: resolution compares die faces directly against static DCs or opposed rolls, using Die Step-Up, Die Step-Down, Boons, and Banes rather than linear numerical modifiers.

Canonical Design Pillars

Mathless Core Resolution

Step pools such as 2dX keep highest.
Fixed DCs from 2 to 12.
Opposed rolls by highest face and tie-breaking procedures.
Boons add same-size dice; Banes remove dice or force worse results.
No linear +1, -2, BAB, ability modifiers, or circumstance stacking.

Simulationist Tactical Play

Three-action turns plus a Free Guard reaction.
Active defenses, paired defenses, Damage Absorption, wounds, hit locations, and combat maneuvers.
Specific skills, activities, tools, equipment, and class permissions.
Rabble, Underlings, and Iconic Champions for practical enemy management.

Zero Meta-Currencies

No Fate Points, Hero Points, Inspiration, Luck Points, or narrative tokens.
In-world resources include Vitality, Stamina, Essence, Vancian Spell Slots, and Equipment Durability.

Universal Actor Schema

Every actor uses:
Race/Ancestry + Background/Origin + Class/Prestige Classes + Skills + Feats.
The schema applies to PCs, NPCs, monsters, bosses, and underlings.

High Fantasy Progression

Trained: Local, Levels 1–4.
Veteran: Regional, Levels 5–8.
Master: Country, Levels 9–12.
Hero: World, Levels 13–16.
Legend: Cosmic, Levels 17–20.
Mythic: Divine, Level 21+.
Canonical Architecture Highlights
Skills and Domains

The canonical skill architecture uses functional Domains containing specific transferable skills:

Combat Mastery.
Athletics, Movement, and Survival.
Subterfuge and Perception.
Knowledge and Technical Practice.
Lore and Cultural Familiarity.
Social and Influence.
Magic Mastery.
Craft and Production.

Activities such as Investigation, Forgery, Disguise, Escape Artistry, Lockpicking, Trap Disarming, Shadowing, Treaty Negotiation, and Interrogation select appropriate skills by method rather than becoming universal skills.

Magic

Magic uses separate axes:

Schools: Eight D&D-compatible technical classifications.
Traditions: Modular magical access and specialization packages.
Mantles: Conceptual domains expressed by magic.
Traits: Practical delivery and interaction descriptors.

Traditions are individual skills with fixed shared spell lists. Classes and Prestige Classes grant Tradition access and spell-acquisition methods; they do not own separate spell lists.

Alchemy is governed by Knowledge and Craft rather than being a Magic Mastery Tradition. Psychic/Psionic power is provisionally a separate Essence-based supernatural system.

Spell Slots

All ordinary spellcasters use one shared daily Spell Slot pool.

Spell Slot Advancement: A level-by-level entry on a class table granting one advancement.
Spell Slot Progression Level: The character’s accumulated position on the Reference Good Slot Progression.
Reference Good Slot Progression: The universal table showing spell slots at Progression Levels 1–20.

Full classes advance every class level, Mediocre classes every other level, and Bad classes every four levels. Every Base Class and Prestige Class displays its actual Spell Slot Advancements level by level.

# [AGENTS.md](http://AGENTS.md) — Agent Operating Guide (Process, Governance, and Repo Protocol)  


**Purpose:** Enable effective continuation of work if chat history is lost.  
**Non-goal:** This file contains no system mechanics, balance targets, or specific design decisions. Those live in canonical docs, the decision log, and the outstanding definitions index. If a sentence here starts describing what the game does rather than how to work on the project, it belongs elsewhere and should be moved.  
  
---  
  
## 1) What This Repo Is  
  
This repository develops a tabletop RPG ruleset using a mathless-at-the-table philosophy and a simulationist design posture. Documentation is deliberately separated into canonical rules, research/comparative analysis, conversion procedures, brainstorm/decision logs, and archived work.  
  
If you need to know what the rules *are*, do not use this file — follow the source-of-truth hierarchy below.  
  
---  
  
## 2) Source-of-Truth Hierarchy  
  
When sources conflict, resolve in this order:  
  
1. **Explicit user decisions made in the current working session**, even if not yet written down anywhere.  
2. **Canonical rules** — `03_core_baseline_system/`, `04_simulationist_subsystems/`.  
3. **The decision log** — `06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/01_master_brainstorm_log.md`, "Core Design Decisions Log" section.  
4. **The outstanding definitions index** — `06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/03_outstanding_definitions_index.md`.  
5. **Research, comparative analysis, and simulations** — `02_comparative_system_analysis/`, `06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/02_probability_and_dice_simulations.md`.  
6. **Conversion procedures** — `05_conversion_and_content_engine/`.  
7. **Archive** — `07_archive/`.  
  
**Rules:**  
  
- Archived or deprecated material is retained for reference only and must never override canonical rules, regardless of how detailed, polished, or recent it looks.  
- Do not infer authority from a document's age, length, or level of detail. A short recent canonical entry outranks a long, old, elaborate one.  
- If nothing in this hierarchy resolves the question, treat it as **open** and present options rather than deciding silently.  
  
---  
  
## 3) Decision Status Vocabulary  
  
Every significant design question carries one of three statuses. This file does not track individual statuses — the outstanding definitions index does — but every agent must use this vocabulary consistently:  
  
- **Locked** — settled architecture. Do not revisit without a strong reason and explicit user approval.  
- **Provisional** — direction accepted; implementation or balance details still open.  
- **Open** — undecided; must be discussed and resolved before implementation.  
  
Consult `06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/03_outstanding_definitions_index.md` for the current status of any given question. Do not infer status from how confidently or informally a document is phrased.  
  
---  
  
## 4) Repository Map (Roles, Not Contents)  
  
```text  
01_design_philosophy_and_pillars/     Design philosophy and pillars — non-canonical context  
02_comparative_system_analysis/       Research, comparisons, external-system studies, simulations  
03_core_baseline_system/              Canonical core rules  
04_simulationist_subsystems/          Canonical subsystem rules  
05_conversion_and_content_engine/     Procedures for porting content from reference systems  
06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/    Decision log, outstanding definitions index, roadmap, sim notes  
07_archive/                           Superseded/historical documents, retained for provenance  

Operational rule: If you change a rule, edit the canonical rules first. Then update the decision log and outstanding definitions index to match. Never let the log/index describe a state the canonical docs don't actually reflect.

5) First-30-Minutes Reading Procedure

For any new agent, or after any loss of context:

Read README.md for current structure and navigation.
Read 06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/03_outstanding_definitions_index.md to learn what is unresolved.
Skim 06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/01_master_brainstorm_log.md for recent decisions relevant to your task.
Read the specific canonical file(s) governing the subsystem you will touch.
Only then consult research, comparative, or conversion documents as needed.

Do not begin implementation work — writing new subsystems, rewriting architecture — before completing step 4.

6) Agent Behavior Expectations

Be conservative with authority.
Do not decide major architecture by implication. If a change touches a foundational assumption, present alternatives and get explicit approval before treating anything as settled.

Prefer small, traceable changes.
Make the minimal edit that achieves the intended result. Avoid broad rewrites unless the task explicitly calls for one. When replacing content, move the old version to 07_archive/ rather than deleting it.

Don't duplicate canon.
Never copy rules, mechanics, or terminology definitions into meta-documents — including this one. Link to the canonical file instead.

7) Design-Change Protocol

Before proposing or applying a change with any real weight:

Locate the canonical home for the rule or subsystem in question.
Search the repo for related terms and prior discussion.
Check the outstanding definitions index for related open items.
Classify the change:
Editorial/clarification — no protocol needed beyond a normal edit.
Mechanical tweak within an existing framework — proceed, but note it in the decision log.
Architectural change — high risk; requires explicit user approval.
For architectural changes:
Present at least two viable options, not a single default.
Explain trade-offs: complexity, internal consistency, conversion impact, drift risk.
Do not silently overturn a Locked decision — flag the conflict and let the user decide.
Get explicit approval before treating any direction as locked.
8) Decision-Recording Protocol

A decision is not real until it is recorded. When a change is approved:

Update the relevant canonical rules document — this is the actual source of truth.
Add or update an entry in the decision log 06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/01_master_brainstorm_log.md, Core Design Decisions Log section), with a new DEC-### identifier.
Update the outstanding definitions index — mark the item resolved, or split it into remaining sub-questions.
Update any research, comparative, or conversion document that referenced the prior open/unresolved state.
Update README.md only if top-level structure or navigation changes.
Move superseded documents to 07_archive/ rather than leaving contradictions sitting in active directories. Include a short note on why it was archived and what replaced it.

Rule: If a decision changes player-facing behavior, it must exist in canonical rules and be traceable via a decision-log entry. Neither alone is sufficient.

9) Terminology Governance
Canonical terminology lives in canonical documents, not here and not in a second shadow glossary.
Before introducing a new term, check whether one already exists for the concept.
If a new term is genuinely needed, define it once, in the correct canonical location, and note it in the decision log.
When encountering outdated terminology in an existing document:
If the document is canonical, update the term.
If the document is research, comparative, or archived, label the terminology as historical rather than editing it away — those documents are allowed to preserve old thinking.
Do not resolve a terminology inconsistency across multiple documents on your own initiative — flag it, unless explicitly asked to fix it.
10) Research and Simulation Standards

When a claim depends on probability, pacing, or balance:

Prefer a small simulation, enumerated table, or explicit calculation over informal reasoning.
Record assumptions, method, results, and interpretation limits alongside the artifact.
Store simulation scripts and outputs in 02_comparative_system_analysis/ or 06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/02_probability_and_dice_simulations.md, not inside canonical rule files.
Treat results as evidence supporting a decision, not as the decision itself — a proposal built on simulation still requires explicit approval.
Never promote an untested probability claim to canonical status.
11) Documentation Style Rules

Canonical documents should be:

Declarative ("is / does"), not speculative or comparative.
Single-source-of-truth — no duplicate copies of the same rule elsewhere.
Explicit about procedures and edge cases.
Linked outward to research for rationale, rather than embedding long justifications inline.

Non-canonical documents should be:

Clearly labeled by kind (research, comparative, brainstorm, historical).
Allowed to contradict canon, since they are not rules.
Explicit about their own status (draft, superseded, historical) where relevant.

Archive policy:

Archive superseded documents rather than leaving them adjacent to canon.
Include a short note explaining why it was archived and what replaced it.
12) Reading-Order and Roadmap Pointers

Build a task-specific reading list using the procedure in Section 5 rather than relying on a fixed list — canonical documents and priorities will change over time, and a hardcoded reading order here would go stale.

Current priorities, in-progress items, and open questions are tracked in:

text
06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/03_outstanding_definitions_[index.md](http://index.md)  
06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/01_master_brainstorm_[log.md](http://log.md)  

This file is not the roadmap and should not be edited to reflect shifting priorities.

13) Completion Checklist

Before marking any non-trivial task done:

 Canonical rules updated, if rules changed.
 Decision-log entry created or updated, if the change was non-trivial.
 Outstanding definitions index updated.
 Cross-references updated (README, related docs) only where actually necessary.
 Superseded content archived or clearly labeled historical.
 No new contradictions introduced across canonical files.
14) Common Failure Modes to Avoid
Treating brainstorm notes or research as if they were canon.
Copying rules or terminology into meta-files, including this one.
Making an architectural change without a corresponding decision-log entry.
Leaving multiple contradictory "canonical" descriptions of the same thing in different places.
Quietly reviving an archived mechanic without re-approval.
Introducing terminology drift — the same concept under two different names.
Inferring a document's authority from its age, length, or apparent thoroughness rather than from Section 2.
Skipping the alternatives-and-trade-offs step for a change that turns out to be architectural.
15) Maintaining This File

Update 
AGENTS.md
 when:

The authority relationship between directories changes.
The design-change or decision-recording protocol itself changes.
A new category of canonical document is introduced.

Do not update 
AGENTS.md
 when:

A game rule, mechanic, or term changes — that belongs in canonical docs.
A decision is resolved — that belongs in the decision log and outstanding definitions index.
Roadmap priorities shift — that belongs in 06_brainstorming_logs_and_roadmap/.
Final Rule

Do not infer authority from a file's age, length, or level of polish. If a claim cannot be traced to canonical rules, the decision log, or an explicit decision made in the current session, treat it as open, present alternatives, and ask for direction rather than deciding silently. This file tells you how to find and use the real sources of truth — it never substitutes for them.

Declarative, not speculative.
Single-source-of-truth.
Explicit about procedures and edge cases.
Linked outward to research for rationale.
Non-canonical documents

Should be:

Clearly labeled as research, comparative, brainstorm, or historical.
Allowed to contradict canon because they are not rules.
Explicit about draft or superseded status where relevant.
Archive policy

Archive superseded documents rather than leaving them adjacent to canonical rules. Include a short explanation of why they were archived and what replaced them.

Before marking a non-trivial task complete:

 Canonical rules updated, if rules changed.
 Decision-log entry created or updated, if non-trivial.
 Outstanding definitions index updated.
 Necessary cross-references updated.
 Superseded content archived or labeled historical.
 No contradictions introduced across canonical files.
14) Common Failure Modes

Avoid:

Treating brainstorm notes or research as canon.
Copying rules or terminology into meta-files.
Making architectural changes without decision-log entries.
Leaving multiple contradictory canonical descriptions.
Reviving archived mechanics without re-approval.
Introducing terminology drift.
Inferring authority from age, length, or polish.
Skipping alternatives and trade-offs for architectural changes.
15) Maintaining This File

Update AGENTS.md only when:

Authority relationships between directories change.
The design-change or decision-recording protocol changes.
A new category of canonical document is introduced.

Do not update it when:

A game rule or mechanic changes.
A decision is resolved.
Roadmap priorities shift.

Those changes belong in canonical documents, the decision log, the outstanding definitions index, or the roadmap.

Final Rule

Do not infer authority from a file’s age, length, or polish. If a claim cannot be traced to canonical rules, the decision log, or an explicit decision made in the current session, treat it as open, present alternatives, and ask for direction rather than deciding silently.

What are the main mechanical pillars of our system so far?

Main Mechanical Pillars
1. Mathless Step-Pool Resolution

The core engine avoids table-side arithmetic.

Characters roll pools such as:

text
2dX keep highest

where:

Attribute determines die size.
Competency Rank determines pool volume and Competency Floor.
Class, feats, tactics, equipment, and conditions provide discrete permissions or Boons/Banes.
Results compare directly against fixed DCs or opposed rolls.

The system avoids linear modifiers such as:

text
+2 attack
-4 Power Attack
+3 circumstance bonus
+BAB
+Ability Modifier
2. Die Steps, Boons, Banes, and Floors

The main resolution tools are:

Die Step-Up: d8 → d10.
Die Step-Down: d10 → d8.
Boons: Add same-size dice, such as 2d8 + 1B → 3d8 keep highest.
Banes: Remove dice or force worse results.
Competency Floors: Training can prevent results below a fixed threshold.

Competency is independent from Character Level.

text
Untrained: Floor 0
Trained: Floor 3
Expert: Floor 5
Master: Floor 7
Legendary: Floor 9
3. Six-Attribute Foundation

The system retains the classic six attributes:

Strength
Dexterity
Constitution
Intelligence
Wisdom
Charisma

Attributes primarily determine die size and physical or mental potential.

They also derive resources and defenses, such as:

Vitality.
Stamina.
Essence.
Fortitude.
Reflexes.
Willpower.
4. Universal Actor Schema

Every actor is constructed from the same five building blocks:

text
Race/Ancestry
Background/Origin
Class and Prestige Classes
Skills
Feats

This applies to:

PCs.
Human NPCs.
Goblins.
Ogres.
Dragons.
Bosses.
Underlings.
Other monsters.

The difference between a PC and a monster is primarily in their selected building blocks and presentation, not in completely unrelated rules.

5. High Fantasy Tier Progression

The game uses 20 character levels across five mortal tiers, plus Mythic advancement:

Tier	Levels	Scope
Trained	1–4	Local
Veteran	5–8	Regional
Master	9–12	Country
Hero	13–16	World
Legend	17–20	Cosmic
Mythic	21+	Divine

Tier boundaries provide major advancement opportunities, while levels inside each tier provide incremental progress.

6. Three-Action Tactical Economy

Each character receives:

text
[A] [A] [A] + [1R] Free Guard

Actions can be used for:

Attacking.
Striding.
Casting.
Drawing or using equipment.
Maneuvers.
Defensive actions.
Tactical positioning.
Multi-action abilities.

Movement uses five spatial tiers:

text
Close
Near
Medium
Far
Distant

One Stride shifts exactly one distance tier.

7. Active Defenses and Layered Protection

The system replaces one universal Armor Class with multiple defenses.

Core defensive layers include:

Reflexes.
Parry.
Fortitude.
Willpower.
Damage Absorption.

The paired defenses are:

text
Fortitude: Strength + Constitution
Reflexes: Dexterity + Intelligence
Willpower: Wisdom + Charisma

Damage Absorption is resolved after a successful attack rather than functioning as a universal hit-avoidance number.

8. Differential Combat and Wounds

Combat is not merely damage against a large pool of hit points.

The system uses:

Opposed attack and defense rolls.
Multi-success outcomes.
Maneuvers.
Natural critical hits.
Called shots.
Anatomical wound conditions.
Damage Absorption.
Vitality loss.
Conditions such as Prone, Concussion, Bleed, and impaired limbs.
Natural Critical

A natural weapon critical:

Deals increased Vitality loss.
Rolls randomly on the anatomical wound matrix.
Produces a severe location-based condition.
Called Shot

A Called Shot:

Does not deal double damage.
Lets the attacker choose the body part.
Applies the corresponding anatomical condition.

These are deliberately different mechanics.

9. Universal Combat Maneuvers

Maneuvers are available to everyone rather than being locked behind large feat chains.

Examples include:

Trip.
Disarm.
Shove.
Grapple.
Overextend.
Bleed.
Called Shot.

They are triggered through:

Multi-success results.
Dedicated maneuver actions.
Deliberate trade-offs such as accepting a Bane.

This preserves Mythras-style tactical agency while retaining the mathless pool engine.

10. In-World Resources Instead of Meta-Currencies

The system has no out-of-world reroll or narrative currencies.

Important in-world resources include:

Vitality.
Stamina.
Essence.
Spell Slots.
Equipment Durability.
Provisions and other campaign resources.
Stamina

Used for:

Physical exertion.
Active defensive effort.
Martial surges.
Die Step-Ups.
Strenuous movement.
Essence

The renamed magical/supernatural resource.

Used for:

0th-Circle spells.
Metamagic.
Casting stability.
Emergency casting.
Turn or Rebuke Undead.
Smites.
Devotion Feats.
Other supernatural features.

Essence remains separate from Stamina.

11. Specific Skills Organized into Domains

Skills represent transferable areas of competence, not individual procedures.

Current Domains include:

Combat Mastery.
Athletics, Movement, and Survival.
Subterfuge and Perception.
Knowledge and Technical Practice.
Lore and Cultural Familiarity.
Social and Influence.
Magic Mastery.
Craft and Production.

Activities such as:

Investigation.
Forgery.
Disguise.
Lockpicking.
Trap Disarming.
Escape Artistry.
Shadowing.
Treaty Negotiation.
Interrogation.
Camp Fortification.

use one or more relevant skills, tools, Lore, Knowledge, class abilities, and feats rather than automatically becoming standalone skills.

12. Domain Architecture

Domains are more than organizational headings.

They may eventually interact directly with:

Class features.
Prestige Classes.
Feats.
Equipment.
Prerequisites.
Domain actions.
Monster design.
Training and advancement.

However, Domains currently do not provide a second proficiency rank. Individual Skills remain the source of check competence.

13. Modular Class and Prestige-Class Advancement

Classes and Prestige Classes are level-banded but use level-by-level tables.

Every class table may define:

Vitality progression.
Combat progression.
Defense progression.
Skill allocations.
Spell Slot Advancements.
Tradition access.
Spell acquisition.
Essence features.
Feats and class abilities.

Prestige Classes use the same mechanical framework as Base Classes. Their distinguishing feature is access requirements.

14. Spellcasting as Shared Vancian Magic

Ordinary spellcasters use:

One universal preparation system.
One shared daily Spell Slot pool.
Spell Circles.
Fixed spell lists by Tradition.
Class-based spell acquisition methods.

Classes do not own separate spell lists.

A Cleric’s Death spells and a Wizard’s Death spells come from the same Death Tradition list.

15. Spell Slot Progression

Classes grant Spell Slot Advancements in their level-by-level tables.

The total accumulated advancements determine the character’s:

Spell Slot Progression Level

That value selects the row on the Reference Good Slot Progression.

Examples:

text
Full caster:
  Advances every class level.

Mediocre caster:
  Advances every other class level.

Bad caster:
  Advances every four class levels.

Noncaster:
  Does not advance Spell Slot Progression.

Multiclassing adds all completed Spell Slot Advancements from all classes and Prestige Classes.

16. Multi-Axis Magic Classification

Each spell can have several classifications:

text
School
Tradition(s)
Mantle(s)
Trait(s)
Schools

The eight D&D-compatible technical schools:

Abjuration.
Conjuration.
Divination.
Enchantment.
Evocation.
Illusion.
Necromancy.
Transmutation.
Traditions

Traditions determine magical access and specialization.

Examples include:

Arcane.
Divine.
Nature.
Spirit.
Shadow.
Elemental.
Rune.
War.
Dream.
Life.
Death.
Eldritch/Void.
Time.
Space.
Chaos.
Order.
Creation.
Mantles

Mantles express conceptual domains such as:

Life.
Death.
Creation.
Fate.
Time.
Conflict.
Guardian.
Knowledge.
Natural World.
Elements.
Force.
Justice.
Repose.
Traits

Traits describe practical use:

Fire.
Healing.
Area.
Projectile.
Touch.
Ritual.
Sustained.
Summoning.
Mind-Affecting.
Reaction.
Movement.

A spell may belong to multiple Traditions while retaining one technical School.

17. Alchemy and Psychic Power

Alchemy is not a magical Tradition.

It is governed by:

Knowledge — Alchemy and Pharmacology.
Craft — Alchemy.
Tools.
Reagents.
Downtime.
Equipment.

Psychic/Psionic power is provisionally a separate Essence-based supernatural system rather than ordinary Vancian Magic Mastery.

18. Enemy and Encounter Scaling

The system supports three broad enemy-management categories:

Rabble: Fast, disposable opponents.
Underlings: Simplified enemies with limited durability.
Iconic Champions: Full actors using the complete rules.

This keeps encounters tactically meaningful without requiring every enemy to track a full PC-style resource and wound structure.

19. Conversion and Compatibility

The system is designed to convert material from:

D&D 3.5e.
Pathfinder 1e and 2e.
Shadow of the Demon Lord.
Weird Wizard.
Mythras/BRP.
Gloomhaven.
Other d20, OSR, and tactical systems.

Conversion preserves conceptual identity while translating mechanics into:

Die sizes.
Pool volumes.
Floors.
Boons and Banes.
Traits.
Actions.
Conditions.
Resource costs.
Spell Schools and Traditions.
Overall Mechanical Identity

In one sentence:

This is a high-fantasy, class-and-skill-driven tactical RPG using mathless step pools, opposed defenses, modular advancement, shared Vancian spellcasting, specific domains of competence, layered wounds, and in-world resource pressure.
